content.text:
Good question, and it changes the calculus from the workflow's earlier verdict — that one concluded "don't build a new plugin yet, no real workload." A real UI build for Lumen *is* that workload, so I'd revisit toward standing up a proper plugin rather than just bolting extensions onto `proof`/`canon`.

**On naming:** the existing set — `axiom`, `basis`, `canon`, `delta`, `graph`, `lambda`, `proof`, `trace`, `vector` — is a consistent register: single abstract nouns from math/logic/formal-systems vocabulary, each a *metaphor* for the plugin's role rather than a literal description of its domain (`lambda` isn't about functional programming, it's "the thing that executes"; `graph` isn't about literal graphs, it's "the structure of need/relationships"). Nothing in that list is domain-literal ("frontend", "ui-kit") and nothing is artsy ("muse", "palette", "canvas" — the last one would also collide with the harness's own built-in `design` skill). So: no, this shouldn't go artsy. It should find the same kind of formal/metaphorical noun, picked for the *role* — bridging one design intent across multiple faithful representations (Figma, tokens, code) — not for "UI" itself.

My top candidates, all real math/physics nouns at the same register as the others:

- **`prism`** — one input refracted into a spectrum of faithful outputs (and recombinable back). Closest metaphor to Curtis's "multiple origins, one hub, lossless bidirectional transforms" idea. My pick.
- **`lattice`** — structural/order-theory term; evokes grids, spacing scales, token hierarchies — leans more toward the systemization side than the multi-representation side.
- **`facet`** — simpler than prism, same idea (one gem, many faces = one component, many views).

options.label: Break convention going forward
options.description: Stop coining clever abstract nouns for new plugins. Name the new FE/design plugin literally (e.g. "ui" or "component"), and future plugins too — accept the ecosystem becomes a mix of abstract (legacy) and literal (new) names.

options.label: Full rename pass
options.description: Treat this as reason to rename all plugins to literal, self-describing names (spec, plan, implement, verify, ship, research, requirements, bugs, scaffold) in one pass — highest disruption, but solves memorability for good and is a one-time cost while adoption is still small.

Based on the web search results, I found relevant information about CLI tool naming conventions and the broader debate between abstract/evocative versus descriptive/literal naming approaches for product families.

## Key Findings

**Naming Approaches for CLI Tools:**

Thoughtful meaninglessness is completely fine and might even be your best option if you expect your command's solution domain to evolve. For example, at smallstep, they use the step and step-ca commands for their public key encryption toolkit and certificate authority.

**Evocative vs. Descriptive Naming Strategies:**

Product naming generally falls into several categories: descriptive naming (names that clearly describe the product's function), and evocative naming (names that evoke an emotional response or imagery, like "Apple" or "Nike").

**Product Family Branding Implications:**

A tool can be named for clarity and speed, while a platform needs a name that can hold weight as the business scales, expands, and eventually means more than what it started as. Calendly is perfectly descriptive — it's clearly related to a calendar and works for scheduling, but imagine Calendly expanding into a full enterprise workflow suite — the name doesn't stretch. In contrast, Stripe was named for something abstract and universal and has grown into payments infrastructure, financial products, tax tools, and more — the name made room.

This demonstrates that the choice between abstract and literal naming conventions significantly impacts a product family's long-term branding flexibility and scalability.

content.text:
Good instinct to check — the umbrella name already exists. The README's masthead reads "**Orin** Agent Plugins" and it's already framed as *"Nine cooperating plugins covering the full development lifecycle."* You don't need to invent a family name — you have one, it's just not doing the memorability work it could be.

**What the research actually supports:**
- The Stripe-vs-Calendly comparison ([Tanj, naming a SaaS brand](https://tanj.co/2026/05/29/naming-a-saas-brand)) is the relevant lesson: literal/descriptive names run out of room as scope grows; abstract names ("Stripe" started as payments, now spans tax/financial infra) age better precisely *because* they don't overpromise a fixed meaning. You already made that bet 9 plugins deep — reversing it now trades a real cost (every `<plugin>:<skill>` invocation, marketplace listing, doc, and your own muscle memory) for a memorability fix that abstract-name ecosystems solve a different way anyway.
- [smallstep's "Poetics of CLI Command Names"](https://smallstep.com/blog/the-poetics-of-cli-command-names/) explicitly defends "thoughtful meaninglessness" for exactly this kind of case — a name that doesn't over-commit to one literal meaning survives the tool's scope evolving.
- HashiCorp — the closest real analog (Terraform/Vault/Consul/Nomad/Packer/Boundary, all abstract single words) — didn't solve memorability by renaming products. They solved it by **grouping into named categories** (their current split is Infrastructure vs. Security) so a user picks a category first, then only needs to recall 2-3 names within it, not 6+ cold.

**So: don't rename the 9, and don't go literal for the 10th either — fix the lookup problem instead.** Concretely:

1. Add an explicit category layer on top of the existing lifecycle diagram — e.g. **Define** (graph, trace) → **Design** (canon, + new plugin) → **Build** (vector, lambda) → **Verify** (axiom, proof) → **Ship** (delta), with **basis** as the cross-cutting meta tier. Right now the README only has the mermaid flow — add a compact table version too (renders without mermaid, scannable in `CLAUDE.md` and every plugin's own README) so "which of 10 words do I need" collapses to "which of 5 bands, then 1-2 names."
2. The new plugin slots into **Design**, next to `canon` — same category, sibling relationship, which itself becomes a memory aid ("canon specs behavior, `<new>` specs components").
3. Keep the new name abstract, same well as before. My pick stands: **`lattice`** — structural/order-theory term, reads naturally as "the grid/composition counterpart to canon," no collision.

Want me to go with `lattice`, or land on one of `facet`/`topology`/`mesh` — and should I add that category-band table to the README/CLAUDE.md now regardless of which name you pick?

content.text:
Yes — "muse" is more whimsical, and that's exactly the register mismatch. `axiom`, `basis`, `canon`, `delta`, `graph`, `lambda`, `proof`, `trace`, `vector` are all formal/structural terms — none of them evoke creativity or inspiration, they evoke mechanism. "Muse" reads as the *source of* a design (inspiration), not the *verification or specification of* one, which is what this plugin would actually do — so it'd also be a weaker functional metaphor, not just a tonal outlier.

If you want to lean whimsical on purpose, that's a legitimate different direction, but it'd be worth doing consistently rather than as one odd plugin out. My honest read: stick with the structural family (`lattice` is still my pick) unless you're ready to reconsider the whole ecosystem's tone, not just this one name.

content.text:
Since you're going all-in: here's a coherent whimsical set, each word chosen so a stranger could guess the plugin's job without decoding a math term first — that's the actual fix for "boring," not just prettier words.

| Current | Role | Proposed | Why it reads |
|---|---|---|---|
| `graph` | capture/structure raw need | **loom** | weaves scattered requirement threads into structure |
| `trace` | research before deciding | **lantern** | lights the unknown before you commit |
| `canon` | draft/gate the spec | **oracle** | issues the definitive, testable pronouncement |
| `vector` | sequence the plan | **atlas** | maps the route, step by step |
| `lambda` | TDD implementation | **smith** | forges the thing, hands-on |
| `proof` | adversarial bug hunting | **sleuth** | hunts down what's hidden |
| `axiom` | cross-cutting verification gate | **sentinel** | guards the gate, nothing passes unchecked |
| `delta` | commit/PR/release | **courier** | delivers the finished work |
| `basis` | meta-plugin, scaffolds/audits | **warden** | keeper of the conventions |
| *(new)* | component/design specs | **muse** | your idea — now it actually fits, since the family isn't formal anymore |

Two notes on choices: I swapped away from the obvious "hound" for the bug-hunter (Hound CI is a real, similarly-scoped code-review bot — too close) and away from "keeper" for the meta-plugin (Keeper Security is a well-known password manager) — **sleuth** and **warden** land the same idea without the collision.

content.text:
Stepping back from bee imagery to what these actually are — a swarm of specialized helper-spirits, each doing one job for you — Roman/Greek mythology actually has a term family built exactly for this: personal guiding/guardian spirits, always spoken of as multiple, each attached to a specific thing they watch over.

- **Numen** (Latin) — an indwelling guiding spirit/presiding power. Bonus: it phonetically echoes **Lumen** already in your family, which is a nice unplanned pairing (light + guiding presence).
- **Genii** (Latin, plural of *genius*) — in Roman belief, every person/place/undertaking had its own attendant guardian spirit (a *genius*). A "genii" is literally a collection of personal helper-spirits, each assigned to watch over one thing — which maps almost exactly onto "ten agents, each with its own craft, all quietly assisting you."
- **Lares** (Latin) — household guardian spirits, always worshipped as a group, protecting and helping the home/family. Same "collective of helpful spirits" idea as Genii, slightly warmer/more domestic connotation, less risk of being misread the way "Genius" alone would be (boastful).

My pick: **Genii** — it's the most literal match to "a set of helpful assistants, each with their own domain," it's plural by nature (so it never needs an "-s" tacked on awkwardly), and it sidesteps the modern "genius = smart person" reading since the plural form isn't the common usage.

Which of these lands, or is there a different angle in this same spirit-helper family you'd rather explore?

content: Think from the perspective of a user triggering the skills and agents

content.text:
Good lens — and it surfaces a real risk I hadn't weighed properly: someone landing cold on a GitHub repo full of `loom`, `sleuth`, `oracle`, `courier`, `muse` with no context reads it as a fantasy-RPG roster before they read it as a serious dev tool, and a name like `muse` in particular could get mistaken for "generates mockups" (which collides with Claude Code's own built-in `design` skill) rather than "specs and audits components" (what it'd actually do).

But going back to literal names throws away the actual win here, so that's not the fix. The fix is **decoupling what a first-time reader needs from what a daily user needs**: a newcomer doesn't decode names, they read whatever's immediately next to the name. So:

- The README's above-the-fold content should lead with **function first** — the lifecycle/category table (Define → Design → Build → Verify → Ship) — before the character names ever appear, so the frame ("this is a spec-driven dev pipeline") is set before anyone meets "the Sleuth."
- Every surface where a name appears alone today — `plugin.json` description, `marketplace.json`, README table, `--help`-equivalent — must pair name + one-line job tag, always, no bare names. This was already true of the current repo's plugin descriptions (they lead with role, e.g. "Cross-cutting verification gate...") — that discipline just needs to survive the rename, not get lost to cleverness.
- `muse` specifically needs its role tag to explicitly rule out the mockup-generation reading on first contact — lead with "specs and audits" not "designs."

content.text:
Good angle — and it surfaces something concrete: right now, 5 of the current plugins are single-skill and the skill name just mirrors the plugin name (`proof:proof`, `trace:trace`, `vector:vector`, `axiom:axiom`, `lambda:lambda`). Carried forward with the new persona names, that becomes `sleuth:sleuth`, `lantern:lantern`, `sentinel:sentinel` — a stutter that reads fine with dry technical nouns but sounds odd with punchier character words, and worse, it wastes the invocation on repeating the *who* instead of saying the *what*.

The fix: split the two jobs cleanly. **Plugin name = who** (the persona/brand — what makes it memorable and fun). **Skill name = what** (the literal action — what the person typing actually needs at that moment, no memorization required). This isn't a new convention — canon/delta/graph already do it (`canon:draft-spec`, `delta:release`) — it just needs to extend to the 5 that currently don't:

| Plugin (persona) | Skill (action) | Invocation |
|---|---|---|
| sleuth | audit | `/sleuth:audit` |
| lantern | research | `/lantern:research` |
| atlas *(or its replacement)* | plan | `/atlas:plan` |
| sentinel | gate | `/sentinel:gate` |
| smith | implement | `/smith:implement` |

Read out loud, each one is self-explanatory at the point of use — "gate this via the sentinel," "implement this with the smith" — so a person typing it (or me, selecting an agent) never needs "sentinel = gate" memorized as a separate fact; the phrase carries both halves. Natural-language trigger phrases (the actual most common invocation path — "find bugs," "spec this out") are untouched by any of this since they match on SKILL.md description text, not the codename, so this only helps and can't hurt that path.

Want me to lock this in — persona names as plugin ids, literal action names as the skill dirs for those 5 — before I move to planning the actual rename?

message.content: Does herald make sense in its position? I also don't like warden. That prison narrative is not the vibe

content.text:
Good gut checks on both.

**Herald** — on reflection, it's a partial fit at best: a herald *announces* a decision already made elsewhere, it doesn't *author* one. Canon's actual job is drafting the binding, testable spec text itself, then gating it — authorship plus judgment, not proclamation. Alternatives that carry the authorship half better:
- **Scribe** — writes the official, binding record. Weaker on the "gates/judges" half, but that's arguably fine since Sentinel already owns hard gating elsewhere in the family, and canon's own gate is closer to "final polish before proceeding" than "the" gate.
- **Arbiter** — has final, definitive say over what's valid — strong on judgment, weaker on authorship.
- My honest lean: **Scribe**, since drafting is canon's primary and most distinctive job; the judgment half is secondary.

**Warden** — agreed, that's a guard-tower/incarceration read, wrong tone entirely for "maintains standards across a growing collection." Better fits, none punitive:
- **Mason** — ties directly to `basis` meaning "foundation": a mason lays foundations to exacting standard *and* historically worked within a guild that enforced strict craft conventions among its members — matches both halves of basis's job (scaffolds new plugins, audits the rest for conformance) more precisely than any option so far.
- **Curator** — maintains and organizes a collection to a consistent standard, no punitive edge, clean fit for "audits every plugin for conformance."
- **Steward** — trusted caretaker managing something on others' behalf, warm connotation, generic fit rather than a sharp one.

We've decided to build a real new plugin, currently code-named "muse" (final public name will be "Muse" per the Wisp rename — see the naming conversation in context), in the agent-plugins repo at /Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins. It sits in the "Design" category alongside canon (renaming to "Scribe"), and Gabe will be using it for real UI work on a project called Lumen.

Context you should know: earlier in this session, a multi-agent research workflow investigated whether a dedicated FE/design plugin was justified at all, and its adversarial critique REJECTED building one — it rejected a `component-spec@1` schema, a `component-architect` agent, and a whole `swatch` plugin, all for the same reason: no demonstrated real workload existed. It recommended only narrow extensions instead: (1) an accessibility hazard taxonomy added to proof's (now "Ranger's") scanner/adversary pipeline, (2) design-token drift smells added to canon's (now "Scribe's") smells reference used by canon:architect, (3) one paragraph of component-criterion drafting guidance added to canon's (now "Scribe's") drafter agent.

That verdict is now STALE — Gabe has since confirmed a real workload exists (building Lumen's UI), which was exactly the missing precondition the critique named. Your job is to design what Muse should actually contain now that the precondition is met, NOT to re-argue whether it should exist.

Do this rigorously:

1. Read /Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/shared/constitution.md in full — this is the hard fence: 5-part agent structure (<constitution>/<backstory>/<goal>/<judgment>/<output>), byte-identical <constitution> section across every agent, EARS placement rules, model/effort tiering (haiku/low for mechanical, sonnet/medium for analysis/execution, opus/high for judgment), Schema-Driven Handoffs (schema must exist in shared/schemas/ BEFORE agent prompts reference it), Subsystem Compilation Batching, Epistemic Stopping (cap adversarial revision at 2 rounds), Reference Files (split by concern, 120-line cap), Skill Names (single lifecycle-stage word by default).

2. Read plugins/canon/ in full (all agents, plugin.json, README.md, and shared/schemas/spec@1.json, shared/schemas/verdict@1.json) as the closest structural template — canon is a sibling "Design" category plugin that also does draft→audit→gate on a spec-like artifact. Also read plugins/proof/ in full (all agents) as the second-closest template, since UI component hazard-scanning has a similar recon→scan→verify shape.

3. Decide: does Muse need a genuinely new schema (e.g. component-spec@1, extending or sibling to spec@1) to represent props/variants/states/accessibility criteria that spec@1's free-text acceptance_criteria can't adequately express? Ground this decision in an actual read of shared/schemas/spec@1.json's acceptance_criteria shape — don't assume either way. If a new schema is warranted, sketch its shape (fields, required, additionalProperties: false, a reasoning scratchpad field per constitution's schema rules).

4. Propose Muse's full agent roster. Right-size it: don't propose more agents than the actual job needs (recall canon has 6 agents because it has 6 genuinely distinct skills; proof has 5 because it has 5 distinct cognitive modes in one pipeline). For each proposed agent give: name, role, model/effort tier with justification, one-sentence job description, and which cognitive mode it occupies (distinguish it clearly from every other agent in the roster — no two agents should do overlapping judgment, per the constitution's cognitive-mode separation implicit in Progressive Context Loading & JIT Hooks: "WHILE an agent is in pattern-matching mode (scanner), it SHALL NOT filter, analyze, or verdict matches").

5. Propose Muse's skill(s) — following the Skill Names rule (single lifecycle-stage word by default, unless that fails to communicate scope).

6. Propose the plugin.json shape (id: "muse", version starting point, description, skills, agents list).

7. Self-critique your own proposal adversarially before finalizing: for each agent, could it be merged into another without losing a genuine cognitive-mode distinction? Is any agent redundant with something Ranger or Scribe already does (re-read plugins/proof/agents/*.md and plugins/canon/agents/*.md specifically for overlap)? Does every EARS-notation sentence you'd write actually belong only in <constitution> or <output> per the EARS Placement rule? Would basis's (Mason's) auditor pass this plugin on a conformance check?

Report back: the final schema decision (with the schema sketch if warranted), the final agent roster table, the skill(s), the plugin.json sketch, and a short list of what you rejected during self-critique and why (so Gabe can see the discipline was applied, not skipped).

input.name: rename-completeness-check
input.description: Enumerate every rename touchpoint for the Wisp naming
input.prompt:
We've decided on a full rename of the agent-plugins repo's plugin family (at /Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins) to a new persona-based naming scheme, umbrella-branded "Wisp":

graph → Weaver
trace → Vanguard
canon → Scribe
vector → Navigator
lambda → Smith
proof → Ranger
axiom → Sentinel
delta → Courier
basis → Mason
(plus a new plugin, "Muse", being designed separately — do not worry about its internal content, just note it as a new addition to plugins/)

Your job is NOT to execute the rename. Your job is to produce a COMPLETE, concrete checklist of every place in the repo that needs to change, so nothing gets missed when the rename is actually executed later. Be exhaustive and specific — file paths and, where useful, line numbers or grep patterns, not vague categories.

Systematically check and report on each of these surfaces:

1. Directory structure: plugins/<old-id>/ for each of the 9 — confirm each needs `git mv` to plugins/<new-id>/.
2. Each plugin's own plugin.json: id field, and whether description text references the old id/name anywhere.
3. Each plugin's own agents/*.md files: read every one and grep for (a) the plugin's own old name appearing in its <backstory>/<goal>/<judgment>/<output> prose, (b) references to OTHER plugins by their old id (e.g. does a lambda agent mention "canon" or "axiom" by name in its prompt text — cross-plugin references are the highest-risk spot for missed renames).
4. Each plugin's own skills/*/SKILL.md files: same cross-reference check, plus check the skill's frontmatter/description for old-name mentions and for the `<plugin>:<skill>` invocation examples they document.
5. marketplace.json and .claude-plugin/ — every place plugin ids or paths are declared.
6. Root-level docs: README.md (the pipeline mermaid diagram, the plugin table, install instructions using `orin-dx/agent-plugins/<id>`), CLAUDE.md (Quick Reference commands), ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, SECURITY.md — grep each for the 9 old plugin ids and report exact hits.
7. Each plugin's own README.md and CHANGELOG.md — confirm whether historical CHANGELOG entries should be left alone (they're a historical record) versus the README which should be updated, per constitution "Documentation" rules.
8. shared/constitution.md itself, shared/references/*.md, shared/schemas/*.json — grep for any of the 9 old plugin ids appearing in schema descriptions or reference file examples.
9. scripts/*.sh — check whether any check script hardcodes a plugin id list (vs. deriving it from `plugins/*/` globbing) — a hardcoded list would silently stop checking a renamed plugin if missed.
10. .github/workflows/*.yml — CI referencing plugin ids or paths.
11. docs/adr/ — note whether a new ADR should be authored documenting this rename decision, per the repo's existing ADR practice (don't write it, just flag it as a needed artifact).
12. Version bump implications: per shared/constitution.md, does renaming a plugin's id count as a breaking change requiring a major version bump in each affected plugin.json (and the root marketplace.json), and does scripts/check-versions.sh's logic (read it) still pass afterward?

For each finding, report: file path, exact line number(s) or grep match, old value, what it needs to become. Group the final report by surface (matching the numbered list above) so it can be used directly as an execution checklist. Do not skip low-looking-risk files — cross-plugin references buried inside agent prompt prose are exactly the kind of thing that's easy to miss and constitution explicitly calls "Tool Language"/EARS-adjacent hygiene issues.

<result>Task: design Muse's schema decision, agent roster, skill(s), and plugin.json for the agent-plugins repo, then adversarially self-critique the proposal. Read shared/constitution.md (already in context), spec@1.json, verdict@1.json, finding-report@1.json, all of canon's and proof's agents/plugin.json as templates.

## Schema decision: no new schema

`spec@1.acceptance_criteria` is already an array of free-text testable-proposition strings with `is_error_case`/`judgment_call` flags — nothing about that shape is backend-specific. A component criterion ("when `disabled=true`, the button renders `aria-disabled=\"true\"` and does not fire `onClick`") is exactly as expressible as an API criterion. Inventing `component-spec@1` now would force every downstream consumer (Navigator, Smith, Sentinel) to learn a second spec shape for zero expressive gain — pure cost. **Muse produces `spec@1` and `verdict@1`, same as Scribe (canon).** Revisit only if real Lumen usage hits a criterion shape free text genuinely can't express (e.g. a state-transition table) — not before.

## What Muse does NOT do: scan implementation code

Muse's own brief says "specs and audits UI components." Read literally that risks rebuilding Ranger's (proof's) recon→scanner→adversary→exit-gate hazard pipeline a second time for accessibility hazards — a direct capability duplication. That work correctly stays on Ranger (add an a11y hazard taxonomy reference + wire it into Ranger's default scan/adversary routing, per the earlier session's still-valid recommendation). **"Audits" in Muse's scope means audits the *spec*, not the *code*** — same split as Scribe auditing specs vs. Ranger auditing code. This needs to be explicit in Muse's plugin.json description or it'll get misread.

## Agent roster (3 agents — deliberately smaller than canon's 6)

| Agent | Model/Effort | Cognitive mode | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| `drafter` | sonnet/medium | authorship | Drafts a component spec@1 from a requirement/design intent — props, variants, per-state observable behavior, accessibility criteria as testable propositions |
| `auditor` | sonnet/medium | adversarial review of the artifact, non-binding | Applies Scribe-auditor's generic tests (testable, unambiguous, no padding) *plus* UI-specific completeness checks (missing interactive states, missing ARIA criteria, invalid prop combinations not marked as error cases) |
| `exit-gate` | opus/high | binding terminal judgment | Default-fail gate before the spec proceeds to Navigator; same retry_count/escalate-at-3 pattern as every other exit-gate in the ecosystem |

Canon's other three agents (`verifier`, `architect`, `drift-checker`) are deliberately **not duplicated**:
- `architect` (finding-report@1 → structural spec@1) is domain-agnostic already — a UI architectural finding routes to Scribe's existing architect, not a new one.
- `drift-checker` (spec@1 vs. workspace) is domain-agnostic already — it works on a component spec exactly as written today with zero changes.
- `verifier` (criterion grounded in requirement@1?) is deferred, not rejected — real risk it catches (drafter inventing ungrounded criteria to please a stakeholder) is much lower for a single-user workload building Lumen directly. Add it later if drift/scope-creep is actually observed, not preemptively.

## Skill

Single skill, `muse:component` (not `muse:muse`) — matches this session's persona=who/skill=what convention, and the constitution's own carve-out ("if a single word does not communicate what the skill acts on, use a more specific word") for the same reason `post-review` beat `post`.

## plugin.json sketch

```json
{
  "id": "muse",
  "name": "muse",

## Muse: proposed design

**No new schema.** `spec@1`'s free-text `acceptance_criteria` already expresses component behavior fine ("when `disabled=true`, renders `aria-disabled="true"` and doesn't fire `onClick`" is just as testable as a backend criterion). Muse produces `spec@1` and `verdict@1` — same schemas as Scribe. Inventing `component-spec@1` now would just force every downstream consumer to learn a second shape for no expressive gain.

| Agent | Tier | Job |

<result>## Rename checklist — restating task

**Headline risk**: cross-plugin references are not rare — they are the dominant content of this repo's docs. Every plugin's README, every CHANGELOG (9 plugin-level + 1 root), `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, the constitution, and roughly a dozen agent/skill prompt files name other plugins by their bare old id in running prose (not just in tables). A naive find-replace on directory names + `plugin.json` alone will leave the repo internally inconsistent in dozens of places.

---

### 1. Directory structure
`git mv plugins/{graph,trace,canon,vector,lambda,proof,axiom,delta,basis} plugins/{weaver,vanguard,scribe,navigator,smith,ranger,sentinel,courier,mason}` — 9 moves. Plus create `plugins/muse/` fresh (separate design task).

### 2. Each plugin's own `plugin.json`
`id` and `name` fields at line 2–3 of every one of the 9 `plugins/<id>/plugin.json` files — both currently equal the old id, both need the new persona word. `version` also needs a bump (see §12). No plugin's own `description` field references its *own* old id by name (they describe function, not name), so no self-referential text fix needed there — but `trace`'s description explicitly says `"...for consumption by canon (spec)"` (`plugins/trace/plugin.json:5`) — cross-reference, needs `canon`→`scribe`.

### 3. Cross-plugin references inside `agents/*.md` prompt bodies — highest risk, easy to miss
Concrete hits found (not exhaustive of every mention, but every file identified):

- `plugins/canon/agents/exit-gate.md:7` — `"...halts progression to vector..."` → `navigator`
- `plugins/canon/agents/drift-checker.md:66` — `"...a new lambda task..."` → `smith`

Every plugin with split skills documents `<plugin>/<skill-name>` inline constantly:

- `plugins/canon/skills/correct-spec/SKILL.md:4,23` — `"lambda"`, `"vector"`, `"challenger"`, `"lambda"` → `smith`, `navigator`
- `plugins/canon/skills/gate-spec/SKILL.md:21,25,38` — `"vector"` → `navigator`

- Root `marketplace.json`: each plugin object has `id`, `name`, `path` (`./plugins/<id>`) — all 9 need updating, plus `trace`'s `description` field (line ~46) contains `"...for consumption by canon (spec)."` → `scribe`, and `lambda`'s description mentions "the axiom exit gate" → `sentinel`.

- Root `marketplace.json`'s top-level `description` ("Nine cooperating plugins...") in `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` also literally says "Nine cooperating plugins covering the full development lifecycle" — becomes 10 once `muse` lands; update count.

Every single row needs the new id.

Per constitution's Documentation section, **README.md must be updated** (it's the live, current-state doc) — every one of the 9 plugin READMEs is saturated with self-referential `<oldid>/<skill>` invocation examples (e.g. `canon/README.md` alone has ~25 such mentions) and cross-plugin "feed X to [other-plugin]" links.
**CHANGELOG.md entries should be left untouched** — they are historical record of what happened under the old names, consistent with how this repo already treats history (e.g. it never rewrites past entries when a skill is renamed, per the extensive `graph/CHANGELOG.md`, `canon/CHANGELOG.md` etc. precedent of documenting renames as new entries, not editing old ones). The rename itself should get **one new CHANGELOG entry per plugin** (and one root entry) documenting old-id → new-id, matching the repo's own established pattern for prior renames (`bug-hunter-rust → proof`, `agent-plugin-builder → basis`, both documented as changelog entries, never scrubbed from history).

### 8. `shared/constitution.md`, `shared/references/*.md`, `shared/schemas/*.json`
- `shared/constitution.md`: line 100 section header "Axiom Retry Caller Constraint" → "Sentinel Retry Caller Constraint"; lines 110, 134, 136, 142 reference `canon`/`planner`/`vector` by name in EARS rules → must become `scribe`/`navigator`; line 160 "`lambda` executes a plan@1" → `smith`; line 236 "`basis:scaffolder` and `basis:auditor`" → `mason:scaffolder`/`mason:auditor`. Lines 152, 171 ("blocker delta", "delta patches") are **not** the plugin — false positives, leave alone (confirmed by reading context).
- `shared/references/workspace-conventions.md:3,9,11,15` — names `canon:auditor, graph:auditor, trace:recon`, and `vector`/`lambda` by id — all four need updating; this file is explicitly `<load_first>`-loaded by multiple agents, so it's high-traffic.
- `shared/references/conventional-commits.md:47-55` — a literal scope table mapping `graph|trace|canon|vector|lambda|proof|axiom|delta|basis` to "`<id>` plugin and subagents" — every row needs the new id (commit scope conventions will otherwise reference dead plugin names forever).
- `shared/references/interface-implementers.md:3` — "`vector:challenger`" → `navigator:challenger`.
- `shared/references/boundary-value-shapes.md:3` — "`lambda:implementer`... proof and reviewer do not..." → `smith:implementer`, `ranger`.

## Wisp — the Lifecycle Ecosystem

Ten plugins, each a specialist persona covering one stage of the development lifecycle — together they're **Wisp**. Each produces a typed output schema consumed by the next stage. They're composable: install only the personas your workflow needs.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef define fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1,stroke-width:2px,color:#1e1b4b,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef design fill:#f5f3ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,stroke-width:2px,color:#4c1d95,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef build fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#3b82f6,stroke-width:2px,color:#1e3a8a,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef verify fill:#fffbeb,stroke:#f59e0b,stroke-width:2px,color:#78350f,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef ship fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#10b981,stroke-width:2px,color:#064e3b,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef meta fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#0f172a,rx:8px,ry:8px;

    we[Weaver\nneed] -->|"requirement@1"| va[Vanguard\nresearch]
    va -->|"research-report@1"| sc[Scribe\nspec]
    sc -->|"spec@1"| na[Navigator\nplan]
    na -->|"plan@1"| sm[Smith\ncode]
    sm -->|"changeset@2"| co[Courier\nship]
    co -. iterate .-> we

    mu[Muse\ncomponent spec] -->|"spec@1"| na

    se([Sentinel\ngate])
    sc -.->|"spec@1"| se
    sm -.->|"changeset@2"| se
    se -.->|"verdict@1"| co

    ra([Ranger\naudit]) -.->|"finding-report@1"| co
    ra -.->|"finding-report@1"| sc
    ma([Mason\nmeta]) -. scaffold .-> we

    class we,va define
    class sc,mu design
    class na,sm build
    class se,ra verify
    class co ship
    class ma meta
```

Grouped by what each persona actually does — five bands across the lifecycle, plus one that stands outside it and maintains the rest:

**Define** — turns a raw idea into something the pipeline can act on
| Persona | Job | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [`weaver`](./plugins/weaver/) | Captures and structures scattered need into requirements | `requirement@1` |
| [`vanguard`](./plugins/vanguard/) | Goes first — researches prior art, risk, and patterns before anyone commits to a direction | `research-report@1` |

**Design** — drafts and gates the authoritative, testable contract
| Persona | Job | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [`scribe`](./plugins/scribe/) | Drafts and gates the unambiguous, binding spec | `spec@1` |
| [`muse`](./plugins/muse/) | Drafts and gates component specs — props, variants, per-state behavior, accessibility | `spec@1` |

**Build** — sequences the plan and makes it real
| Persona | Job | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [`navigator`](./plugins/navigator/) | Decomposes the spec into an exact, step-by-step plan | `plan@1` |
| [`smith`](./plugins/smith/) | Implements via TDD — failing test, minimal code, green, commit | `changeset@2` |

**Verify** — nothing proceeds without evidence
| Persona | Job | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [`sentinel`](./plugins/sentinel/) | Cross-cutting gate — confirms any artifact meets its criteria before the next stage begins | `verdict@1` |
| [`ranger`](./plugins/ranger/) | Hunts down real bugs through adversarial, evidence-based verification | `finding-report@1` |

**Ship** — carries the finished work out
| Persona | Job | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [`courier`](./plugins/courier/) | Commits, opens PRs, responds to review, writes changelogs and release notes | `release-artifact@2` |

**Meta** — maintains the family itself, outside the sequence
| Persona | Job | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [`mason`](./plugins/mason/) | Lays the foundation — scaffolds new plugins, audits the rest for conformance | — |

Ten plugins, each a specialist persona covering one stage of the development lifecycle — together they're **Wisp**. Each produces a typed output schema consumed by the next stage. They're composable: install only the personas your workflow needs.

```mermaid

    classDef build fill:#eff6ff,stroke:#3b82f6,stroke-width:2px,color:#1e3a8a,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef verify fill:#fffbeb,stroke:#f59e0b,stroke-width:2px,color:#78350f,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef ship fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#10b981,stroke-width:2px,color:#064e3b,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef meta fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#0f172a,rx:8px,ry:8px;

    we[Weaver\nneed] -->|"requirement@1"| va[Vanguard\nresearch]

    sc -->|"spec@1"| na[Navigator\nplan]
    na -->|"plan@1"| sm[Smith\ncode]
    sm -->|"changeset@2"| co[Courier\nship]
    co -. iterate .-> we

    mu[Muse\ncomponent spec] -->|"spec@1"| na

    ma([Mason\nmeta]) -. scaffold .-> we

    class we,va define
    class sc,mu design
    class na,sm build
    class se,ra verify
    class co ship

**Design** — drafts and gates the authoritative, testable contract
| Persona | Job | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

| [`muse`](./plugins/muse/) | Drafts and gates component specs — props, variants, per-state behavior, accessibility | `spec@1` |

**Build** — sequences the plan and makes it real
| Persona | Job | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

| Persona | Job | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [`sentinel`](./plugins/sentinel/) | Cross-cutting gate — confirms any artifact meets its criteria before the next stage begins | `verdict@1` |
| [`ranger`](./plugins/ranger/) | Hunts down real bugs through adversarial, evidence-based verification | `finding-report@1` |

**Ship** — carries the finished work out
| Persona | Job | Output |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

| Persona | Job | Output |

content.content:
# Lumen Repository Overview

## Project Summary
Lumen is a Rust-based analytics engine for AI coding agents that parses session transcripts, calculates prompt cache economics using Anthropic's pricing model, and detects circular tool-use patterns via graph analysis. It supports multiple agent orchestrators (Claude Code, Antigravity, Codex, OpenCode).

## Visual & Design Style

### Color Palette
The documentation employs a deliberate semantic color system:

- **Indigo/Purple**: Primary actions and engine components (`#6366f1`, `#8b5cf6`)
- **Amber/Orange**: Router/detection logic (`#f59e0b`)
- **Slate/Gray**: Data storage layers (`#64748b`)
- **Emerald/Green**: Terminal output and success states (`#10b981`)
- **Neutral grays**: Backgrounds and muted text (`#f8fafc`, `#0f172a`)

### Typography & Structure
The README uses:
- **Bold headers** with markdown hierarchy (`##`, `###`) for scannable sections
- **Monospace code blocks** for CLI examples and function signatures
- **Tables** (via `comfy-table`) with consistent cell alignment for metrics display
- **ASCII flowcharts** and Mermaid diagrams for architecture visualization

### Design Tokens & Conventions
- **Border radius**: `8px`–`10px` for component grouping in diagrams
- **Stroke width**: `1.5px`–`2px` for visual hierarchy
- **Icons/badges**: SVG shields for CI status, license, and Rust version
- **Table styling**: "Rounded" box-drawing characters (`╭`, `┆`, `╰`) for terminal UI readability

### UI Aesthetic
Clean, technical minimalism emphasizing data transparency—no gradients, soft shadows, or decorative flourishes. The design prioritizes legibility for engineering audiences and terminal-native output formats.

content.text:
Draw as the engineer who has to live with the decision, not as a decorator: a diagram earns its place when it lets a cold reader see a mechanism they would otherwise have to assemble from prose - where data flows, which components talk, what changes between two options, what state a request moves through. If a sentence says it faster, write the sentence.

## What to draw

**Depict the mechanism, not its name.** A box labeled "cache" says less than the prose; the path a request takes through it, the two stores it sits between, and the arrow that disappears when the cache is removed say what the words can't. Show the parts that the argument hinges on - the boundary being crossed, the hop being added, the data that moves - and leave out the parts that don't.

**Comparing options?** Draw the difference. Two architectures side by side, a before and an after, the one edge that each option adds or removes - the reader should be able to point at what they are choosing between. A separate labeled box per option, with nothing connecting them to the system, is not a comparison; it is a restated option list.

**Match complexity to the stakes.** A one-hop question is a three-box diagram; a migration that reroutes writes through a queue needs the queue, the writer, the reader, and the ordering arrow. Draw as much as the decision actually turns on - no forced minimalism, no inventory of the whole system either.

**Label the arrows.** An unlabeled arrow is "related somehow"; `writes`, `invalidates`, `polls every 30s` is information. A legend is only worth it when the same encoding (dashed, colored, doubled) repeats; otherwise put the meaning on the mark itself.

## Inline SVG mechanics

These mechanics apply where the page renders inline SVG natively (HTML pages); a markdown-rendered page draws its diagrams in whatever fence that lane's renderer supports, and the skill that owns the lane says which. Hand-author inline `<svg>` with native shapes (`rect`, `circle`, `line`, `polyline`, `path`) and `<text>` - no libraries, no runtime, no external images.

- **Size by `viewBox`.** Set `viewBox="0 0 W H"` and let CSS scale it (`max-width: 100%; height: auto`); choose W and H for the content, not a preset. Wide flows read left-to-right; layered stacks read top-to-bottom.
- **Theme with `currentColor`.** Strokes, text, and arrowheads in `currentColor` inherit the page's foreground in light and dark themes alike; reserve a literal hue for the one element that carries meaning (the option leaned toward, the hop under discussion), and make sure it reads on both grounds.
- **Arrowheads are markers or polygons.** A `<defs><marker>` referenced by `marker-end="url(#arrow)"` (fragment-internal id) or a small `<polygon>` at the line's end - never an image.
- **Keep text legible.** Roughly 11-13px at the drawn scale, `text-anchor` for alignment, short labels (a word or three); explanatory sentences belong in the caption below the figure, not in the drawing.
- **Align to a grid.** Shared baselines and even gaps are most of what makes a hand diagram read as deliberate; eyeballed offsets read as noise.
- **One figure, one claim.** Wrap the `<svg>` in `<figure>` with a `<figcaption>` that states what the picture shows, and give the `<svg>` `role="img"` plus an `aria-label` carrying the same claim for readers who cannot see it.
- **Stay self-contained.** No `<script>`, `<style>`, or `<foreignObject>` inside the SVG; gradients, patterns, and `<use>` reference ids in the same fragment (`href="#id"`). Long decorative path data is a sign the drawing wants a real graphics tool - simplify instead.

Loaded the diagramming skill for grounded principles rather than freehand guesses. Translating its rules to a Mermaid-in-GitHub context (not inline SVG, so some mechanics don't apply, but the underlying design logic does):

**What actually applies here:**
- **Depict the mechanism, not just labeled boxes** — ours already does this: nodes are personas, edges carry the actual schema name being handed off (`spec@1`, `plan@1`), not vague "relates to" arrows. Keep that.
- **Color carries exactly one meaning** — category, and nothing else. No decorative color. Already true after the last edit.
- **Font weight is the wrong lever in Mermaid-on-GitHub.** GitHub's renderer doesn't reliably honor custom font-weight theming — chasing bold/regular distinctions here is fighting a tool that won't cooperate. The right substitute for visual hierarchy is **shape**, which Mermaid does control reliably: we're already using rounded-rect for primary pipeline stages and stadium/pill for verification-and-meta nodes (sentinel, ranger, mason) — that's a real, working hierarchy signal, it just was never stated as a deliberate rule.
- **A legend is only worth it when an encoding repeats** — color now repeats six times (justified, we added it), but there's a second encoding repeating that has no legend yet: **solid edges = primary pipeline flow, dashed edges = verification/meta side-channel**. That's used throughout the diagram silently. Worth naming.
- **Font size**: default Mermaid sizing is fine at this diagram's scale — bumping it would be decoration, not a fix for an actual legibility problem.

content.text:
Yes — and the real problem isn't styling, it's topology. `Ranger` and `Mason` both have long-range feedback edges (Ranger reaches back to `Scribe`, Mason reaches back to `Weaver`, both from the far end of the chain), so in a single left-to-right layout those edges are forced to cross almost the entire diagram no matter how we color or size things. No amount of font/spacing tuning fixes an edge that structurally has to span the whole canvas.

The diagramming skill's actual rule for this is "one figure, one claim" — right now we're bundling two different claims into one picture: *the sequential pipeline* and *the cross-cutting verification/meta layer*. Splitting those into two smaller diagrams would let each one be genuinely clean:

1. **Primary flow** — Weaver → Vanguard → Scribe/Muse → Navigator → Smith → Courier, with the iterate loop. Six nodes, no crossing edges, reads in one glance.
2. **Verification & meta layer** — Sentinel gating Scribe+Smith before Courier, Ranger auditing and feeding back to Scribe, Mason scaffolding/auditing the family. Small, separate, and honest about being a different kind of relationship (checks and maintenance, not sequence).

This also fixes something the current single diagram actually hides: it shows Ranger *producing* findings but never shows what it's auditing (Smith's code) — splitting it out gives room to draw that input honestly instead of cramming it into an already-busy graph.

Want me to do the split, or would you rather keep one diagram and I try repositioning declarations to minimize crossings first (smaller change, won't fully solve it, but doesn't restructure the doc)?

## Wisp — the Lifecycle Ecosystem

Ten plugins, each a specialist persona covering one stage of the development lifecycle — together they're **Wisp**. Each produces a typed output schema consumed by the next stage. They're composable: install only the personas your workflow needs.

73	    sc -->|"spec@1"| na["**navigator**\nplan"]

152	
153	`sentinel` is a reusable, artifact-agnostic verification gate. Any artifact type — spec, plan, changeset, finding report — can be run through it.
154	
155	```mermaid
156	flowchart LR
157	    classDef source fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1,stroke-width:2px,color:#1e1b4b,rx:8px,ry:8px;
158	    classDef store fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#0f172a,rx:8px,ry:8px;

161	    classDef output fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#10b981,stroke-width:2px,color:#064e3b,rx:8px,ry:8px;
162	    classDef alert fill:#fff1f2,stroke:#f43f5e,stroke-width:2px,color:#881337,rx:8px,ry:8px;
163	
164	    Art[artifact + criteria]
165	
166	    subgraph check [Verification Chain]
167	        direction LR
168	        Recon["recon
169	        haiku / low"] --> Ver["verifier
170	        sonnet / medium"] --> Gate["exit-gate
171	        opus / high"]
172	    end
173	
174	    Art --> Recon
175	
176	    Fix["producing agent
177	    targeted patch on blockers
178	    (effort escalates on retry 2)"]
179	
180	    Gate -->|pass| Done(["verdict@1 · pass"])
181	    Gate -->|fail| Fix
182	    Fix -->|"retry ≤ 3 · updated retry_count"| Art
183	    Fix -->|"retry > 3"| Esc(["escalate to human"])
184	
185	    class Art source
186	    class Recon store
187	    class Ver engine
188	    class Gate router
189	    class Done output
190	    class Fix router

194	```
195	
196	On `fail`, the orchestrator passes **only the blockers array** back to the producing agent — not the full artifact context — so it can make a targeted fix. On retry 2, the effort level escalates. After 3 retries, the circuit breaks and control passes to the human.
197	
198	`retry_count` is tracked inside `verdict@1` and incremented by the exit gate on each pass.
199	
200	---
201	
202	## 7. Agent Authoring Principles
203	
204	Full guide: `shared/agent-best-practices.md`. Key constraints:
205	
206	**5-part agent structure** — every agent defines:
207	
208	| Part | Purpose |
209	| :--- | :--- |
210	| **Constitution** | Ecosystem-wide invariants, byte-identical across every agent — the shared cache prefix. Never authored per-agent; copied verbatim. |
211	| **Backstory** | 2–4 sentences of experiential perspective. What has this agent been burned by? What does it value? Guides judgment in the open interior. |
212	| **Goal** | What the agent must produce and why. Intent, not steps. |
213	| **Judgment** | How to know if the goal was genuinely achieved vs. output that looks like it was. Names the key failure mode. |
214	| **Output** | Structured output shape, referencing a schema from `shared/schemas/` when the output flows to another agent. |
215	
216	**Cognitive mode dispatch** — agents are dispatched by the cognitive mode they require, not their pipeline position.
217	- A scanner (exhaustive pattern matching, no filtering) and an adversary (default-to-skepticism, requires a concrete failing scenario) cannot share a mental mode — combining them produces an agent worse at both
218	- Modes: enumeration (haiku/low), tracing/analysis/repair (sonnet/medium), adversarial judgment (opus/high)
219	- A plugin with distinct scanning, tracing, adversarial, and repair phases has a dedicated agent per mode
220	
221	**Progressive context loading** — each agent loads only the reference file for its cognitive phase.
222	- A `<load_first>` block names the specific `shared/references/` file — scanner loads hazards, architect loads smells, mutator loads tooling
223	- Never load all reference files into all agents — attention degrades when the context window contains material the agent won't use
224	
225	**EARS for edges only** — EARS notation (`WHEN`, `IF`, `WHILE`, `WHERE`) belongs in output contracts and never-do rules.
226	- Not in implementation steps or search strategies — those are the interior where agent judgment is the point
227	- Over-constraining the interior caps the agent at the level of the author's imagination
228	
229	**Schema-driven handoffs** — where one agent's output is another's input, both reference the same schema file from `shared/schemas/`. The schema is the contract; the prompt describes the intent.
230	
231	---
232	
233	## 8. Cross-Platform Compatibility
234	
235	Plugins run natively in Claude Code and AGY — no custom server framework required.
236	
237	| Concern | Approach |
238	| :--- | :--- |
239	| Model routing | `model`/`effort` frontmatter for Claude Code; AGY uses its own router |
240	| Tool calls | Abstract language — portable across both platforms |
241	| Paths | Relative only — `shared` symlink provides consistent paths from any plugin dir |
242	| Schema validation | Wiring-time, host-side — agents never validate JSON Schema directly |

    class O router

Use the lowest tier that produces correct output. Opus is reserved for decisions that produce a binding verdict with downstream consequences.

---

## 6. The Sentinel Gate Protocol

`sentinel` is a reusable, artifact-agnostic verification gate. Any artifact type — spec, plan, changeset, finding report — can be run through it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef source fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1,stroke-width:2px,color:#1e1b4b,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef store fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#0f172a,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef engine fill:#f5f3ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,stroke-width:2px,color:#4c1d95,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef router fill:#fffbeb,stroke:#f59e0b,stroke-width:2px,color:#78350f,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef output fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#10b981,stroke-width:2px,color:#064e3b,rx:8px,ry:8px;
    classDef alert fill:#fff1f2,stroke:#f43f5e,stroke-width:2px,color:#881337,rx:8px,ry:8px;

    Art[artifact + criteria]

    subgraph check [Verification Chain]
        direction LR
        Recon["recon
        haiku / low"] --> Ver["verifier
        sonnet / medium"] --> Gate["exit-gate
        opus / high"]
    end

    Art --> Recon

    Fix["producing agent
    targeted patch on blockers
    (effort escalates on retry 2)"]

    Gate -->|pass| Done(["verdict@1 · pass"])
    Gate -->|fail| Fix
    Fix -->|"retry ≤ 3 · updated retry_count"| Art
    Fix -->|"retry > 3"| Esc(["escalate to human"])

    class Art source
    class Recon store
    class Ver engine
    class Gate router
    class Done output
    class Fix router
    class Esc alert

    style check fill:#fafafa,stroke:#cbd5e1,stroke-width:1.5px,stroke-dasharray: 4 4,rx:10px,ry:10px
```

On `fail`, the orchestrator passes **only the blockers array** back to the producing agent — not the full artifact context — so it can make a targeted fix. On retry 2, the effort level escalates. After 3 retries, the circuit breaks and control passes to the human.

`retry_count` is tracked inside `verdict@1` and incremented by the exit gate on each pass.

---

## 7. Agent Authoring Principles

Full guide: `shared/agent-best-practices.md`. Key constraints:

**5-part agent structure** — every agent defines:

| Part | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Constitution** | Ecosystem-wide invariants, byte-identical across every agent — the shared cache prefix. Never authored per-agent; copied verbatim. |
| **Backstory** | 2–4 sentences of experiential perspective. What has this agent been burned by? What does it value? Guides judgment in the open interior. |
| **Goal** | What the agent must produce and why. Intent, not steps. |
| **Judgment** | How to know if the goal was genuinely achieved vs. output that looks like it was. Names the key failure mode. |
| **Output** | Structured output shape, referencing a schema from `shared/schemas/` when the output flows to another agent. |

**Cognitive mode dispatch** — agents are dispatched by the cognitive mode they require, not their pipeline position.
- A scanner (exhaustive pattern matching, no filtering) and an adversary (default-to-skepticism, requires a concrete failing scenario) cannot share a mental mode — combining them produces an agent worse at both
- Modes: enumeration (haiku/low), tracing/analysis/repair (sonnet/medium), adversarial judgment (opus/high)
- A plugin with distinct scanning, tracing, adversarial, and repair phases has a dedicated agent per mode

**Progressive context loading** — each agent loads only the reference file for its cognitive phase.
- A `<load_first>` block names the specific `shared/references/` file — scanner loads hazards, architect loads smells, mutator loads tooling
- Never load all reference files into all agents — attention degrades when the context window contains material the agent won't use

**EARS for edges only** — EARS notation (`WHEN`, `IF`, `WHILE`, `WHERE`) belongs in output contracts and never-do rules.
- Not in implementation steps or search strategies — those are the interior where agent judgment is the point
- Over-constraining the interior caps the agent at the level of the author's imagination

**Schema-driven handoffs** — where one agent's output is another's input, both reference the same schema file from `shared/schemas/`. The schema is the contract; the prompt describes the intent.

---

## 8. Cross-Platform Compatibility

Plugins run natively in Claude Code and AGY — no custom server framework required.

| Concern | Approach |
| :--- | :--- |
| Model routing | `model`/`effort` frontmatter for Claude Code; AGY uses its own router |
| Tool calls | Abstract language — portable across both platforms |
| Paths | Relative only — `shared` symlink provides consistent paths from any plugin dir |
| Schema validation | Wiring-time, host-side — agents never validate JSON Schema directly |

personas, plus a new tenth plugin — memorability had become a real
cost as the ecosystem grew past 9 plugins, and the persona convention
splits "who" (plugin id, a craft-role character) from "what" (skill
name, a literal action), so invocations like `sentinel:gate` and

Single-skill plugins also renamed their skill from the plugin id to
a literal action: ranger/audit, vanguard/research, navigator/plan,
sentinel/gate, smith/implement.

Also adds `muse`, a new Design-category plugin for UI component
specs (props, variants, per-state behavior, accessibility) — reuses
spec@1/verdict@1 rather than a new schema, and explicitly audits the
spec, not the implementation (ranger's accessibility hazard taxonomy
remains the code-level scanning surface).

- Both marketplace files, all plugin.json ids/versions (major bump),

gh pr create --title "feat!: rename plugin family to persona-based Wisp naming, add muse" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary

- Renames all 9 plugins from abstract math/logic nouns to character personas, splitting **who** (plugin id) from **what** (skill name — a literal action):
  `graph→weaver` · `trace→vanguard` · `canon→scribe` · `vector→navigator` · `lambda→smith` · `proof→ranger` · `axiom→sentinel` · `delta→courier` · `basis→mason`
  Single-skill plugins also get literal skill names: `ranger/audit`, `vanguard/research`, `navigator/plan`, `sentinel/gate`, `smith/implement`.
- Adds **muse**, a new Design-category plugin for UI component specs (props, variants, per-state behavior, accessibility). Reuses `spec@1`/`verdict@1` — no new schema — and explicitly audits the *spec*, not the implementation; code-level a11y scanning stays on ranger.
- Redraws the root README and ARCHITECTURE.md lifecycle diagrams: split into a primary-flow diagram and a separate verification diagram (the old single diagram forced ranger's and mason's feedback edges across the whole canvas), plus a consistent color/shape/font-weight system across the repo.
- Reorders all 10 plugin READMEs so decision-relevant sections (When to Use, Install) precede reference material, and refreshes every plugin's pipeline diagram to the same visual language. Mason gets its first diagram (scaffold/audit shown as parallel, not sequential — it isn't a linear pipeline).
- New ADR (`docs/adr/007-wisp-persona-naming.md`) recording the naming rationale for future contributors.

## Why

The ecosystem had grown to 9 plugins named after abstract math/logic terms (axiom, basis, canon, delta, graph, lambda, proof, trace, vector) with no shared mnemonic — memorability was becoming a real cost, not just an aesthetic one. The persona convention fixes this without going fully literal: each plugin id is a distinct character with an obvious craft (a smith builds, a sentinel guards, a courier delivers), and pairing it with a literal skill name means an invocation like `sentinel:gate` or `smith:implement` is self-explanatory without memorizing a mapping table.

## Breaking change

Every renamed plugin's `id` changed — anyone with `orin-dx/agent-plugins/<old-id>` installed needs to reinstall under the new id. All 9 renamed plugins got a major version bump; historical CHANGELOG entries are untouched (new entries document the rename), matching this repo's own precedent for the prior `bug-hunter-rust → proof` rename.

## Test plan

- [x] `./scripts/check-versions.sh` — all versions agree across plugin.json/README/CHANGELOG/marketplace.json
- [x] `./scripts/check-skills-doc.sh` — every documented skill has a matching directory
- [x] `./scripts/check-mermaid.sh` — 18 mermaid blocks across the repo render cleanly

- [x] `jq` valid on both marketplace files and all 10 `plugins/*/plugin.json`
- [ ] Manual look at GitHub's actual Mermaid rendering once this is up (validated locally, but font-weight/size handling in `classDef` can render slightly differently across Mermaid versions)

content.text:
Honest answer: I can produce clean SVG geometry and I understand composition/color principles reasonably well, but logo design specifically is a domain where I'm genuinely less reliable than I am at, say, a technical diagram — a diagram just needs to convey a mechanism clearly, a logo needs to be distinctive and *feel* right, and I can't actually see my own rendered output to judge and iterate the way a designer would. I write the SVG path math blind and hope it composes well.

Two honest paths forward:

1. **I take a real crack at it** — a few "wisp" concept directions (a soft glowing tendril/flame shape, a trail of light with a small spark head, something more abstract/geometric), published as an Artifact so you can actually *see* them and react, treated explicitly as drafts rather than a finished asset.
2. **Use Claude Code's built-in `design` skill** instead — it's purpose-built for this (visual canvas, click-to-select, properties panel, you can refine it by hand afterward), likely a better fit than me hand-authoring raw SVG paths for something this visually load-bearing, since you'd get an editable result rather than a static file you'd have to ask me to blindly re-tweak.

Let me look at what exists first before we pick a direction.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

content.text: # Wisp — Design Brief ## What it is **Wisp** is the umbrella brand for a 10-plugin Claude Code / AGY ecosystem (repo: `orin-dx/agent-plugins`) that helps developers build non-trivial software with AI coding agents without silently dropping requirements as context compresses. The core mechanic: every stage of the dev lifecycle (requirements → research → spec → plan → implementation → verification → shipping) is handled by a specialized plugin that reads/writes typed, versioned artifacts to disk — specs live on disk, agents read from disk, drift is detectable instead of silent. **Audience:** software engineers, mostly senior/technical, installing this inside Claude Code. The tone needs to read as *credible professional tooling* — not enterprise-cold, but also not cartoonish or twee. ## The naming philosophy — why "Wisp" The 10 plugins used to be named after abstract math/logic nouns (axiom, basis, canon, delta, graph, lambda, proof, trace, vector) — technically elegant, but memorability became a real cost once the ecosystem passed 9 plugins. The fix: rename every plugin to a **persona** — a character with an obvious craft — and split "who" (the plugin, a character) from "what" (the skill, a literal action), so an invocation like `sentinel:gate` or `smith:implement` is self-explanatory without memorizing a lookup table. The umbrella name **Wisp** was chosen deliberately from folklore: a *will-o'-the-wisp* is a small, wandering light that leads travelers through uncertain ground in the dark. That's the actual metaphor for the product — each persona is a small guiding light that takes a different shape for a different part of the journey from raw idea to shipped code. It's meant to feel warm, a little magical, and *helpful* — not a cold "AI assistant" glow. Names explicitly rejected along the way, for calibration: `Prism` (collides with another of the founder's own tools), `Guild`/`Forge`/`Atelier`/`Loft`/`Den` (umbrella-name candidates that felt too generic or too try-hard), `Hachi`/`Apis`/`Agora`/`Numen`/`Genii`/`Lares` (too scholarly/dry for the individual persona names), and naming plugins after real famous engineers (a pattern already used elsewhere by this team, deliberately avoided here to stay distinct). ## The ten personas | Category | Persona | Job | |---|---|---| | Define | **Weaver** | Turns scattered raw need into structured requirements | | Define | **Vanguard** | Goes first — researches prior art and risk before anyone commits to a direction | | Design | **Scribe** | Drafts and gates the authoritative, testable spec | | Design | **Muse** | Specs and audits UI components — props, states, accessibility | | Build | **Navigator** | Sequences the spec into an exact, step-by-step plan | | Build | **Smith** | Implements via TDD — failing test, minimal code, green, commit | | Verify | **Sentinel** | Cross-cutting gate — confirms any artifact meets its criteria | | Verify | **Ranger** | Hunts down real bugs through adversarial verification | | Ship | **Courier** | Carries finished work through commit, PR, and release | | Meta | **Mason** | Lays the foundation — scaffolds and audits every other plugin (stands outside the sequence) | Five of these categories form a linear pipeline (Define → Design → Build → Verify → Ship); Mason sits apart, maintaining the family itself rather than being a stage in it. ## What's wrong with the current logo `assets/logo.svg` is a cold cyan/blue "AI tech emblem" — neon glow filters, gradient nodes, a bold all-caps geometric sans wordmark ("ORIN AGENT PLUGINS"). It reads as a generic AI-startup mark and has zero connection to the wisp/guiding-light concept the whole brand is now built around. ## Constraints for the new logo - **Must survive both a white and a near-black GitHub README background.** GitHub does not reliably run CSS `prefers-color-scheme` media queries inside an ``-embedded SVG, so the real deliverable is two files (light-tuned, dark-tuned) served through a `` element — not one SVG trying to self-adapt. - **Avoid the current "AI-generated design" clichés**: purple-to-blue gradient hero glow, neon-emblem tech look, Inter/Space Grotesk as the "safe" display face, generic rounded-lg treatment. - **Warm, not cold.** Ember/candlelight energy — a guiding light over uncertain ground — rather than a sterile blue "AI" glow. - **Credible, not cutesy.** No ghost mascots, no fantasy/wizard-kitsch lettering. This is developer tooling first. - **Should scale down cleanly** — used as a masthead lockup around 300–400px wide, ideally also legible at favicon scale. ## Directions already explored (for calibration, not to be repeated verbatim) Three concepts were drafted and shown to the founder as an Artifact — reactions not yet finalized, but useful signal on the target territory: 1. **Ember Trail** — a single flame shape mid-flicker with a soft curling tail. Most literal to the folklore. 2. **Twin Light** — two small glowing points (one warm, one cool) drifting on a faint shared arc, symbolizing "a family of many small guiding personas" rather than one flame. 3. **Drift Mark** — a minimal line trailing off into a single point of light. Most abstract, most likely to survive at tiny scale. Palette used in the drafts (a starting point, not locked): warm ember gold (`#FFCB7D` → `#D9791F`), a muted dusk violet (`#6E5B9E`) as the cool counterpoint, and warm off-black/off-white neutrals (`#241E2C` / `#F1EBE2`) rather than pure grey.
