#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Extracts every ```mermaid fenced block from every .md file in the repo and
# renders each through @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli. Reports which files/blocks
# fail to parse — a diagram with a syntax error still displays as valid
# markdown, so `git status`/`jq`-style checks never catch this; only an
# actual render does. Needs Node (npx); no repo dependency required, resolved
# on demand.
#
# Usage: scripts/check-mermaid.sh

set -euo pipefail
script_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
# shellcheck source=lib/report.sh
source "$script_dir/lib/report.sh"
cd "$script_dir/.."

workdir="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$workdir"' EXIT

fail=0
count=0

while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
  block_index=0
  in_block=0
  block_content=""
  while IFS= read -r line; do
    if [[ "$line" == '```mermaid' ]]; then
      in_block=1
      block_content=""
      continue
    fi
    if [[ $in_block -eq 1 && "$line" == '```' ]]; then
      in_block=0
      count=$((count + 1))
      mmd="$workdir/block_${count}.mmd"
      printf '%s\n' "$block_content" > "$mmd"
      if ! npx --yes @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli -i "$mmd" -o "$workdir/block_${count}.svg" > "$workdir/log_${count}.txt" 2>&1; then
        fail=$((fail + 1))
        echo "FAIL: $file (block $((block_index + 1)))"

```
[FAIL] Validate  ×5 (all recent runs on main)
```

So this isn't a regression from our rename — it's a pre-existing, unrelated bug: `check-mermaid.sh` shells out to `@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli`, which launches a headless Chrome via Puppeteer. GitHub Actions runners run jobs as root, and Chrome refuses to start its sandbox as root without an explicit `--no-sandbox` flag — the workflow never passes one, so every single diagram in the repo fails identically, regardless of content. Worth fixing since it's currently blocking every PR that touches any markdown file, not just ours.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Extracts every ```mermaid fenced block from every .md file in the repo and
# renders each through @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli. Reports which files/blocks
# fail to parse — a diagram with a syntax error still displays as valid
# markdown, so `git status`/`jq`-style checks never catch this; only an
# actual render does. Needs Node (npx); no repo dependency required, resolved
# on demand.
#
# Usage: scripts/check-mermaid.sh

set -euo pipefail
script_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
# shellcheck source=lib/report.sh
source "$script_dir/lib/report.sh"
cd "$script_dir/.."

workdir="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$workdir"' EXIT

fail=0
count=0

while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
  block_index=0
  in_block=0
  block_content=""
  while IFS= read -r line; do
    if [[ "$line" == '```mermaid' ]]; then
      in_block=1
      block_content=""
      continue
    fi
    if [[ $in_block -eq 1 && "$line" == '```' ]]; then
      in_block=0
      count=$((count + 1))
      mmd="$workdir/block_${count}.mmd"
      printf '%s\n' "$block_content" > "$mmd"
      if ! npx --yes @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli -i "$mmd" -o "$workdir/block_${count}.svg" > "$workdir/log_${count}.txt" 2>&1; then
        fail=$((fail + 1))
        echo "FAIL: $file (block $((block_index + 1)))"
        grep -A2 '^Error' "$workdir/log_${count}.txt" | head -3 | sed 's/^/    /'
      fi
      block_index=$((block_index + 1))
      continue
    fi
    if [[ $in_block -eq 1 ]]; then
      block_content="${block_content}${line}"$'\n'
    fi
  done < "$file"
done < <(find . -name '*.md' -not -path './.git/*' -not -path '*/node_modules/*' -not -path '*/target/*' -print0)

report_check "$fail" "$count" \
  "mermaid block(s) across the repo, all render cleanly." \
  "mermaid block(s) did not render. Fix and re-run."

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Extracts every ```mermaid fenced block from every .md file in the repo and
# renders each through @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli. Reports which files/blocks
# fail to parse — a diagram with a syntax error still displays as valid
# markdown, so `git status`/`jq`-style checks never catch this; only an
# actual render does. Needs Node (npx); no repo dependency required, resolved
# on demand.
#
# Usage: scripts/check-mermaid.sh

set -euo pipefail
script_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
# shellcheck source=lib/report.sh
source "$script_dir/lib/report.sh"
cd "$script_dir/.."

workdir="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$workdir"' EXIT

# CI runners (and some local setups) run as root, where Chrome refuses to
# start its sandbox without this — mermaid-cli's bundled Puppeteer needs it
# passed explicitly via a config file rather than as a CLI flag.
puppeteer_config="$workdir/puppeteer-config.json"
cat > "$puppeteer_config" <<'JSON'
{"args": ["--no-sandbox", "--disable-setuid-sandbox"]}
JSON

fail=0
count=0

while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
  block_index=0
  in_block=0
  block_content=""
  while IFS= read -r line; do
    if [[ "$line" == '```mermaid' ]]; then
      in_block=1
      block_content=""
      continue
    fi
    if [[ $in_block -eq 1 && "$line" == '```' ]]; then
      in_block=0
      count=$((count + 1))
      mmd="$workdir/block_${count}.mmd"
      printf '%s\n' "$block_content" > "$mmd"
      if ! npx --yes @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli -i "$mmd" -o "$workdir/block_${count}.svg" -p "$puppeteer_config" > "$workdir/log_${count}.txt" 2>&1; then
        fail=$((fail + 1))
        echo "FAIL: $file (block $((block_index + 1)))"
        grep -A2 '^Error' "$workdir/log_${count}.txt" | head -3 | sed 's/^/    /'
      fi
      block_index=$((block_index + 1))
      continue
    fi
    if [[ $in_block -eq 1 ]]; then
      block_content="${block_content}${line}"$'\n'
    fi
  done < "$file"
done < <(find . -name '*.md' -not -path './.git/*' -not -path '*/node_modules/*' -not -path '*/target/*' -print0)

report_check "$fail" "$count" \
  "mermaid block(s) across the repo, all render cleanly." \
  "mermaid block(s) did not render. Fix and re-run."

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Extracts every ```mermaid fenced block from every .md file in the repo and
# renders each through @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli. Reports which files/blocks
# fail to parse — a diagram with a syntax error still displays as valid
# markdown, so `git status`/`jq`-style checks never catch this; only an
# actual render does. Needs Node (npx); no repo dependency required, resolved
# on demand.
#
# Usage: scripts/check-mermaid.sh

set -euo pipefail
script_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
# shellcheck source=lib/report.sh
source "$script_dir/lib/report.sh"
cd "$script_dir/.."

workdir="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$workdir"' EXIT

# CI runners run jobs as root, where Chrome refuses to start its sandbox
# without this flag — passed via a puppeteer config file since mmdc has no
# CLI flag for it directly. Scoped to CI only (GitHub Actions always sets
# CI=true): a custom puppeteer config on a local machine can interfere with
# how mermaid-cli resolves an already-cached Chrome binary, so local runs
# keep using mmdc's own default resolution, which needs no such override.
mmdc_args=()
if [[ "${CI:-}" == "true" ]]; then
  puppeteer_config="$workdir/puppeteer-config.json"
  cat > "$puppeteer_config" <<'JSON'
{"args": ["--no-sandbox", "--disable-setuid-sandbox"]}
JSON
  mmdc_args=(-p "$puppeteer_config")
fi

fail=0
count=0

while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
  block_index=0
  in_block=0
  block_content=""
  while IFS= read -r line; do
    if [[ "$line" == '```mermaid' ]]; then
      in_block=1
      block_content=""
      continue
    fi
    if [[ $in_block -eq 1 && "$line" == '```' ]]; then
      in_block=0
      count=$((count + 1))
      mmd="$workdir/block_${count}.mmd"
      printf '%s\n' "$block_content" > "$mmd"
      if ! npx --yes @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli -i "$mmd" -o "$workdir/block_${count}.svg" "${mmdc_args[@]}" > "$workdir/log_${count}.txt" 2>&1; then
        fail=$((fail + 1))
        echo "FAIL: $file (block $((block_index + 1)))"
        grep -A2 '^Error' "$workdir/log_${count}.txt" | head -3 | sed 's/^/    /'
      fi
      block_index=$((block_index + 1))
      continue
    fi
    if [[ $in_block -eq 1 ]]; then
      block_content="${block_content}${line}"$'\n'
    fi
  done < "$file"
done < <(find . -name '*.md' -not -path './.git/*' -not -path '*/node_modules/*' -not -path '*/target/*' -print0)

report_check "$fail" "$count" \
  "mermaid block(s) across the repo, all render cleanly." \
  "mermaid block(s) did not render. Fix and re-run."

content.text:
Good — checked the actual repo state first rather than assuming. Real finding: **Muse already has substantial a11y awareness baked into component-spec drafting** (role, name, focus order, keyboard operability, live-region announcements are explicit criteria requirements) — better than I expected. But **zero code-level a11y scanning exists** (no `shared/references/*-hazards-a11y.md`, Ranger has no a11y taxonomy), **general specs via Scribe have no a11y prompting at all** (Muse only covers "UI components," not CLI tools or general features with user-facing output), and there's **no CLI accessibility consideration anywhere**.

Now dispatching real external research in parallel before I write the proposal.

input.description: Research WCAG and machine-checkable a11y rules
input.prompt:
Research WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) for the purpose of informing how an AI coding-agent pipeline should draft accessibility requirements and scan code for accessibility defects.

Cover, with real sources (search the web, don't rely on memory alone):
1. WCAG 2.2's structure: the four POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust), the three conformance levels (A/AA/AAA), and roughly how many success criteria exist at each level.
2. Which WCAG success criteria are most commonly automatable/machine-checkable (e.g., via axe-core, Lighthouse, pa11y) versus which genuinely require human judgment — this distinction matters because a coding agent can reliably scan for some things (missing alt text, color contrast ratios, missing form labels, heading order) but not others (whether alt text is meaningfully descriptive, whether a workflow is genuinely understandable).
3. How major automated accessibility testing tools (axe-core/Deque, Lighthouse, pa11y, WAVE) structure their rule definitions — look at the actual shape of an axe-core rule (id, description, WCAG success criterion mapping, impact level, selector/matching logic) since this is a good model for how we might define a similar "hazard taxonomy" rule format.
4. WCAG 3.0 (formerly "Silver") — what's different about its draft approach (outcomes-based scoring vs pass/fail) and whether it's stable enough to plan against yet, or still too early-draft.
5. Any recent (2025/2026) guidance specifically about using LLMs/AI agents for accessibility auditing or accessible-by-default code generation — search for this specifically, it's a fast-moving area.

Return a structured findings report: a summary of WCAG's structure usable by someone unfamiliar with it, a list of the most machine-checkable success criteria with their SC numbers (e.g. 1.1.1, 1.4.3, 4.1.2) and what an automated check for each would concretely look for, the axe-core rule shape as a model, and anything found on LLM-assisted a11y auditing. Cite sources.

input.description: Research BBC, NN/g, and leading a11y/UX experts
input.prompt:
Research how leading, widely-respected organizations and practitioners approach accessibility as a design discipline (not just a compliance checklist), for the purpose of informing how an AI coding-agent pipeline should think about accessibility during spec-writing and design, not just code auditing.

Cover, with real sources (search the web, don't rely on memory alone):
1. BBC's accessibility standards and guidelines (they publish "BBC Accessibility Standards and Guidelines" and have historically been a widely-cited public example of an org treating a11y as a first-class product requirement, not an afterthought — find their actual current guidance, and anything about their process for baking accessibility into design/spec stages before code is written).
2. Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g)'s published research and articles on accessibility, specifically anything framing accessibility as inseparable from good UX (search for terms like "accessibility usability", "inclusive design", NN/g's accessibility research reports) — what's their core argument for why accessible design produces better design for everyone, and what process guidance do they give for incorporating accessibility from the start of a design process rather than retrofitting it.
3. Other widely-cited accessibility/inclusive-design practitioners and their core frameworks: Microsoft's Inclusive Design Toolkit/principles, Heydon Pickering's "Inclusive Components" approach, the A11Y Project's checklist philosophy, WebAIM's practical guidance, and any well-known "accessibility acceptance criteria" or "definition of done" templates used by real engineering teams (search for "accessibility acceptance criteria template", "accessibility definition of done").
4. Specifically look for any guidance on writing accessibility requirements as testable/falsifiable acceptance criteria (as opposed to vague statements like "must be accessible") — this is the exact shape we need since our spec-drafting agents require every acceptance criterion to be a testable proposition.

Return a structured findings report covering each source's core contribution, with a focus on: (a) how to write accessibility as testable acceptance criteria at spec time, (b) how to treat accessibility as inseparable from UX quality rather than a compliance bolt-on, (c) any concrete checklists or rule-sets that could inform an agent's judgment. Cite sources.

input.description: Research CLI and terminal accessibility
input.prompt:
Research accessibility specifically for command-line interfaces and terminal applications (NOT web/GUI accessibility — that's covered by a separate research effort). This is a less mainstream area; do real web research rather than relying on memory.

Cover, with real sources:
1. Screen reader compatibility with terminal emulators and CLI tools — what actually breaks (e.g., spinners/progress bars that spam a screen reader, ANSI escape codes read aloud as garbage, TUI applications using ncurses-style full-screen rendering that screen readers can't parse, color-only status signaling).
2. The Command Line Interface Guidelines (clig.dev) — what do they say, if anything, about accessibility, output design for non-visual consumption, and machine-readable output modes.
3. The NO_COLOR movement (no-color.org) and related conventions (FORCE_COLOR, terminal capability detection) — the actual convention and why it matters for both accessibility and scriptability.
4. Known best practices for accessible CLI/TUI design: structured/parseable output modes (--json, --plain), avoiding color as the only signal (also pairing with text/symbols), respecting terminal width and NO_COLOR, providing --help and man pages for discoverability, avoiding interactive-only prompts that block non-interactive or assistive-technology use, exit code conventions, avoiding ASCII art/decorative box-drawing that confuses screen readers, and general "output should degrade gracefully when piped or redirected."
5. Search for any published research, blog posts, or conference talks specifically about "CLI accessibility" or "terminal accessibility" or "accessible developer tools" from 2023-2026 — this is a niche but real area (e.g. look for work from GitHub CLI, terminal accessibility working groups, or accessibility-focused devtool teams).
6. Any known frameworks/libraries for building accessible TUIs (e.g. Textual's accessibility features, accessible terminal UI toolkits).

Return a structured findings report: concrete, checkable rules for CLI accessibility (analogous to WCAG success criteria but for terminal interfaces), citing real sources. ## WCAG Research Findings Report

### 1. WCAG 2.2 structure

WCAG's requirements are organized under four principles, **POUR**:
- **Perceivable** — information/UI must be presentable in ways users can perceive (text alternatives, captions, contrast, adaptable presentation)
- **Operable** — UI and navigation must be operable (keyboard access, timing, seizure avoidance, navigability, input modalities)
- **Understandable** — content and operation must be understandable (readable text, predictable behavior, input assistance)
- **Robust** — content must work with a wide range of current and future user agents/assistive tech (valid parsing, name/role/value exposure)

Three cumulative **conformance levels**: A (minimum) → AA (the level almost all legal mandates, e.g. ADA/EN 301 549, require) → AAA (highest, rarely required site-wide).

**WCAG 2.2 has 86 total success criteria**: 31 at Level A, 24 at Level AA, 31 at Level AAA. Because conformance is cumulative, "AA conformance" = all 31 A criteria + all 24 AA criteria = 55 criteria total. ([W3C WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), [TestParty — 87 SC breakdown](https://testparty.ai/blog/wcag-22-success-criteria-list), [Eye-Able](https://eye-able.com/blog/wcag-a-aa-aaa))

### 2. Automatable vs. judgment-required criteria

Consistent estimate across sources: **roughly 30–40% of WCAG success criteria are reliably machine-checkable**; the rest need a human. Deque's own volume-weighted analysis claims ~57% of *issue instances* (not SCs) are caught by automation — a higher number because a few automatable rules (contrast, alt presence) fire very frequently in the wild — but by *success-criterion* count the automatable fraction is much smaller, and **no SC required for AA can be fully satisfied by automated testing alone** (Deque itself states this). ([Deque WCAG 2.1 support blog](https://www.deque.com/blog/support-for-wcag-2-1-in-axe-core/), [UK Intelligence Community Design System — automated testing limitations](https://design.sis.gov.uk/accessibility/testing/automated-testing-limitation/))

**Most machine-checkable success criteria** (what an automated check concretely looks for):

| SC | Name | What an automated check looks for |
|---|---|---|
| **1.1.1** | Non-text Content | `<img>`/`area`/`input[type=image]` missing `alt` attribute, or empty `alt` on a non-decorative-looking image (presence only — *not* whether the alt text is meaningful) |
| **1.3.1** | Info and Relationships | Missing table headers (`<th>`/`scope`), missing `<label for>`/`aria-label` on form controls, heading level skips (h1→h3), list markup misuse |
| **1.4.3** | Contrast (Minimum) | Computed foreground/background color luminance ratio < 4.5:1 (or 3:1 for large text) — fully algorithmic |
| **1.4.4 / 1.4.10** | Resize Text / Reflow | Fixed px units preventing 200% zoom without horizontal scroll, viewport meta blocking zoom |
| **2.1.1 / 2.4.3** | Keyboard / Focus Order | Elements with `tabindex` > 0, positive tabindex misuse, `onclick` on non-interactive elements with no keyboard handler |
| **2.4.2** | Page Titled | Missing/empty `<title>` |
| **2.4.4 / 2.4.9** | Link Purpose | Empty link text, generic text like "click here" with no accessible name, duplicate link text pointing to different destinations |
| **3.1.1** | Language of Page | Missing/invalid `lang` attribute on `<html>` |
| **4.1.1** | Parsing (deprecated in 2.2 but still checked) | Duplicate IDs, unclosed/malformed tags |
| **4.1.2** | Name, Role, Value | Custom widgets/ARIA roles missing required name/role/state (e.g., `role="button"` with no accessible name), invalid ARIA attribute values, ARIA on unsupported elements |

**Requires human judgment (cannot be reliably automated):**
- Whether alt text is *meaningfully descriptive* vs. just present (1.1.1)
- Whether reading order and focus order make logical *sense* (1.3.2, 2.4.3)
- Whether a workflow, instructions, or error message is genuinely *understandable* (3.3.x, 3.1.5)
- Whether content requiring user input has adequate context/help (3.3.5)
- Meaningful sequence and purpose of gestures/motion (2.5.x)
- Whether captions/audio descriptions are accurate (1.2.x)
- Consistent navigation and identification *in a meaningful sense* (3.2.3/3.2.4) — structurally checkable but semantically judged

### 3. Automated tool rule structures

**axe-core (Deque)** — the most detailed public model. A rule is JSON with: `id`, `impact` (minor/serious/critical, sometimes "moderate"), `selector` (CSS/DOM-path matcher), `matches` (a named function for extra filtering logic beyond the selector), `tags` (WCAG SC mapping like `wcag2aa`, `wcag143`, plus `EN-301-549`, `ACT`, best-practice tags), `actIds` (links to W3C ACT test rules), `metadata.description` / `metadata.help` (human-readable explanation), and `all`/`any`/`none` arrays of atomic **checks** that combine to a pass/fail. Real example (`color-contrast.json`):

```json
{
  "id": "color-contrast",
  "impact": "serious",
  "matches": "color-contrast-matches",
  "excludeHidden": false,
  "tags": ["cat.color", "wcag2aa", "wcag143", "TTv5", "TT13.c",
           "EN-301-549", "EN-9.1.4.3", "ACT", "RGAAv4", "RGAA-3.2.1"],
  "actIds": ["afw4f7", "09o5cg"],
  "metadata": {
    "description": "Ensure the contrast between foreground and background colors meets WCAG 2 AA minimum contrast ratio thresholds",
    "help": "Elements must meet minimum color contrast ratio thresholds"
  },
  "all": [],
  "any": ["color-contrast"],
  "none": []
}
```
This id→impact→WCAG-SC-tag→description→matcher-logic shape is a strong direct model for a "hazard taxonomy" entry: taxonomy_id, severity, SC mapping(s), human-readable description, and a matching/detection rule. ([axe-core rule-development.md](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core/blob/master/doc/rule-development.md), [color-contrast.json](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core/blob/develop/lib/rules/color-contrast.json))

**pa11y** is a runner, not its own engine — it drives headless Chrome via Puppeteer and delegates rule evaluation to a pluggable engine, either **axe-core** or **HTML_CodeSniffer** (WCAG2/Section 508 rulesets); it adds orchestration (CLI/CI config, `pa11y.json`, `--ignore`/`--threshold` flags) but no rules of its own. ([pa11y GitHub](https://github.com/pa11y/pa11y))

**Lighthouse** (Google) wraps axe-core-derived audits into its accessibility category, scoring 0–100 and grouping by impact.

**WAVE** (WebAIM) uses its own proprietary rule engine with icon-based annotations (errors, alerts, features, structural elements, ARIA) overlaid directly on the rendered page rather than a JSON rule export.

### 4. WCAG 3.0 ("Silver")

Still an **early-stage W3C Working Draft** — not stable enough to plan against yet:
- Latest Working Draft published **September 2025** (updated March 2026); explicitly **not a Recommendation** and not to be used for compliance.
- Replaces binary pass/fail SCs with an **outcomes-based scoring model**: each of **174 outcomes** (vs. 86 SCs in 2.2) is scored 0–4 rather than pass/fail.
- Replaces A/AA/AAA with **Bronze/Silver/Gold** conformance; Bronze requires an average score ≥3.5 across all outcomes with the same floor in every functional category.
- Timeline: Candidate Recommendation expected ~late 2027, final publication targeted ~late 2029.
- No law anywhere currently references WCAG 3.0; WCAG 2.x remains the compliance target for the foreseeable future — **do not architect the pipeline around WCAG 3.0's schema yet**, but the outcomes/scoring shift is worth tracking since it changes "pass/fail" into a graded score, which may map better onto an LLM-based hazard-confidence model. ([WCAG 3.0 explainer — webability.io](https://www.webability.io/blog/wcag-3-0-explained), [web-accessibility-checker.com preparation guide](https://web-accessibility-checker.com/en/blog/wcag-3-0-preparation-guide), [accessibility.com — First Public Working Draft](https://www.accessibility.com/blog/silver-wcag-3-0-first-public-working-draft-released))

### 5. LLM/AI-agent accessibility auditing — recent (2025/2026) findings

This is genuinely fast-moving and directly relevant:

- **Microsoft's A11y LLM Eval** (2025/2026, tests GPT-5.x, Claude Haiku/Opus/Sonnet, Gemini 3.x on 32 accessibility test cases across React/Vanilla JS): **baseline LLM-generated code passes only ~12%** of accessibility checks with no guidance; giving models a detailed WCAG 2.2 instruction set raises the pass rate to **~60%** (a 48.5-point jump). Even minimal instructions help (37%). Most common residual failures: color contrast (89% of detected issues), missing ARIA attributes/roles, broken focus management in interactive widgets, and missing helper-text associations. Complex layouts (e.g., shopping pages) scored 0% across all models — implying an agent pipeline needs explicit, structured a11y requirements injected at generation time, not reliance on default model behavior. ([microsoft.github.io/a11y-llm-eval-report](https://microsoft.github.io/a11y-llm-eval-report/))

- **CodeA11y** (CHI 2025, arXiv 2502.10884) — a GitHub Copilot extension using three cooperating LLM agents: a **Responder** (generates accessible code proactively from a system prompt tuned to a11y standards), a **Correction agent** (parses axe DevTools linter output and proposes fixes), and a **Reminder agent** (flags manual-check-only items, e.g. meaningful alt text, that automation can't verify). This maps closely onto a coding-agent pipeline design: generate-with-guidance → automated-scan → LLM-mediated-fix-suggestion → flag-for-human-review on judgment items. Finding: LLM-assisted code can match or exceed human-written accessibility in some cases but still fails on compliance depth; novice developers using AI assistants still omit key practices. ([CodeA11y paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.10884), [CHI 2025 ACM record](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706598.3713335))

- **A11yN** ("aligning LLMs for accessible web UI code generation") — trains/aligns a code-generating LLM via a reward function that penalizes WCAG violations, with penalty severity scaled to violation severity as scored by an accessibility testing engine (i.e., RL/DPO-style alignment against axe-core-style scoring, not just prompting).

- **A11YRepair** (arXiv 2606.21926, "knowledge-enhanced divide-and-conquer repair") and the related "Blind Edits to Verified Repair" work (arXiv 2608.24913) converge on the same architecture recommendation: **never let an LLM patch blind** — apply candidate fix → re-run an automated auditor (axe-core plus computed-style probes) → accept only if detected violations strictly decrease → otherwise roll back and reprompt with the specific violation findings as feedback. This "generate → scan → gate → loop" pattern is the clearest concrete blueprint found for how a coding-agent pipeline should structure its accessibility remediation loop.

- General 2026 framing: audits still find **>90% of public web pages contain detectable violations**; the consensus across these papers is that AI hasn't replaced accessibility specialists but "made their expertise scalable" — i.e., automation should surface candidates and human/specialist judgment should remain the gate for anything above the machine-checkable ~30–40% of criteria.

### Implication for pipeline design

- **Requirements drafting**: for each generated component, inject the machine-checkable SC list (1.1.1 presence, 1.3.1 structure, 1.4.3 contrast, 2.4.2 title, 4.1.2 name/role/value, etc.) as concrete, falsifiable generation constraints — this is what took Microsoft's eval from 12%→60%.
- **Scanning**: model the hazard taxonomy directly on axe-core's rule shape (id, impact, SC-tag, description, matcher) — it's already a proven, widely-adopted format and would let the pipeline optionally shell out to real axe-core/pa11y for the machine-checkable half rather than reinventing detection logic.
- **Judgment items**: don't let the scanner claim confidence on alt-text quality, workflow understandability, or meaningful reading order — flag these explicitly as "needs human/specialist review," mirroring CodeA11y's Reminder agent and A11y LLM Eval's finding that passing automated checks doesn't guarantee WCAG conformance.
- **Repair loop**: adopt the generate→scan→gate(strictly-decreasing-violations)→rollback-and-reprompt pattern from A11YRepair rather than one-shot fixes.</result>

| **2.1.1 / 2.4.3** | Keyboard / Focus Order | Elements with `tabindex` > 0, positive tabindex misuse, `onclick` on non-interactive elements with no keyboard handler |
| **2.4.2** | Page Titled | Missing/empty `<title>` |
| **2.4.4 / 2.4.9** | Link Purpose | Empty link text, generic text like "click here" with no accessible name, duplicate link text pointing to different destinations |
| **3.1.1** | Language of Page | Missing/invalid `lang` attribute on `<html>` |
| **4.1.1** | Parsing (deprecated in 2.2 but still checked) | Duplicate IDs, unclosed/malformed tags |
| **4.1.2** | Name, Role, Value | Custom widgets/ARIA roles missing required name/role/state (e.g., `role="button"` with no accessible name), invalid ARIA attribute values, ARIA on unsupported elements |

**Requires human judgment (cannot be reliably automated):**
- Whether alt text is *meaningfully descriptive* vs. just present (1.1.1)
- Whether reading order and focus order make logical *sense* (1.3.2, 2.4.3)
- Whether a workflow, instructions, or error message is genuinely *understandable* (3.3.x, 3.1.5)
- Whether content requiring user input has adequate context/help (3.3.5)
- Meaningful sequence and purpose of gestures/motion (2.5.x)
- Whether captions/audio descriptions are accurate (1.2.x)
- Consistent navigation and identification *in a meaningful sense* (3.2.3/3.2.4) — structurally checkable but semantically judged

### 3. Automated tool rule structures

**axe-core (Deque)** — the most detailed public model. A rule is JSON with: `id`, `impact` (minor/serious/critical, sometimes "moderate"), `selector` (CSS/DOM-path matcher), `matches` (a named function for extra filtering logic beyond the selector), `tags` (WCAG SC mapping like `wcag2aa`, `wcag143`, plus `EN-301-549`, `ACT`, best-practice tags), `actIds` (links to W3C ACT test rules), `metadata.description` / `metadata.help` (human-readable explanation), and `all`/`any`/`none` arrays of atomic **checks** that combine to a pass/fail. Real example (`color-contrast.json`):

```json
{
  "id": "color-contrast",
  "impact": "serious",
  "matches": "color-contrast-matches",
  "excludeHidden": false,
  "tags": ["cat.color", "wcag2aa", "wcag143", "TTv5", "TT13.c",
           "EN-301-549", "EN-9.1.4.3", "ACT", "RGAAv4", "RGAA-3.2.1"],
  "actIds": ["afw4f7", "09o5cg"],
  "metadata": {
    "description": "Ensure the contrast between foreground and background colors meets WCAG 2 AA minimum contrast ratio thresholds",
    "help": "Elements must meet minimum color contrast ratio thresholds"
  },
  "all": [],
  "any": ["color-contrast"],
  "none": []
}
```
This id→impact→WCAG-SC-tag→description→matcher-logic shape is a strong direct model for a "hazard taxonomy" entry: taxonomy_id, severity, SC mapping(s), human-readable description, and a matching/detection rule. ([axe-core rule-development.md](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core/blob/master/doc/rule-development.md), [color-contrast.json](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core/blob/develop/lib/rules/color-contrast.json))

**pa11y** is a runner, not its own engine — it drives headless Chrome via Puppeteer and delegates rule evaluation to a pluggable engine, either **axe-core** or **HTML_CodeSniffer** (WCAG2/Section 508 rulesets); it adds orchestration (CLI/CI config, `pa11y.json`, `--ignore`/`--threshold` flags) but no rules of its own. ([pa11y GitHub](https://github.com/pa11y/pa11y))

**Lighthouse** (Google) wraps axe-core-derived audits into its accessibility category, scoring 0–100 and grouping by impact.

**WAVE** (WebAIM) uses its own proprietary rule engine with icon-based annotations (errors, alerts, features, structural elements, ARIA) overlaid directly on the rendered page rather than a JSON rule export.

### 4. WCAG 3.0 ("Silver")

Still an **early-stage W3C Working Draft** — not stable enough to plan against yet:
- Latest Working Draft published **September 2025** (updated March 2026); explicitly **not a Recommendation** and not to be used for compliance.
- Replaces binary pass/fail SCs with an **outcomes-based scoring model**: each of **174 outcomes** (vs. 86 SCs in 2.2) is scored 0–4 rather than pass/fail.
- Replaces A/AA/AAA with **Bronze/Silver/Gold** conformance; Bronze requires an average score ≥3.5 across all outcomes with the same floor in every functional category.
- Timeline: Candidate Recommendation expected ~late 2027, final publication targeted ~late 2029.
- No law anywhere currently references WCAG 3.0; WCAG 2.x remains the compliance target for the foreseeable future — **do not architect the pipeline around WCAG 3.0's schema yet**, but the outcomes/scoring shift is worth tracking since it changes "pass/fail" into a graded score, which may map better onto an LLM-based hazard-confidence model. ([WCAG 3.0 explainer — webability.io](https://www.webability.io/blog/wcag-3-0-explained), [web-accessibility-checker.com preparation guide](https://web-accessibility-checker.com/en/blog/wcag-3-0-preparation-guide), [accessibility.com — First Public Working Draft](https://www.accessibility.com/blog/silver-wcag-3-0-first-public-working-draft-released))

### 5. LLM/AI-agent accessibility auditing — recent (2025/2026) findings

This is genuinely fast-moving and directly relevant:

- **Microsoft's A11y LLM Eval** (2025/2026, tests GPT-5.x, Claude Haiku/Opus/Sonnet, Gemini 3.x on 32 accessibility test cases across React/Vanilla JS): **baseline LLM-generated code passes only ~12%** of accessibility checks with no guidance; giving models a detailed WCAG 2.2 instruction set raises the pass rate to **~60%** (a 48.5-point jump). Even minimal instructions help (37%). Most common residual failures: color contrast (89% of detected issues), missing ARIA attributes/roles, broken focus management in interactive widgets, and missing helper-text associations. Complex layouts (e.g., shopping pages) scored 0% across all models — implying an agent pipeline needs explicit, structured a11y requirements injected at generation time, not reliance on default model behavior. ([microsoft.github.io/a11y-llm-eval-report](https://microsoft.github.io/a11y-llm-eval-report/))

- **CodeA11y** (CHI 2025, arXiv 2502.10884) — a GitHub Copilot extension using three cooperating LLM agents: a **Responder** (generates accessible code proactively from a system prompt tuned to a11y standards), a **Correction agent** (parses axe DevTools linter output and proposes fixes), and a **Reminder agent** (flags manual-check-only items, e.g. meaningful alt text, that automation can't verify). This maps closely onto a coding-agent pipeline design: generate-with-guidance → automated-scan → LLM-mediated-fix-suggestion → flag-for-human-review on judgment items. Finding: LLM-assisted code can match or exceed human-written accessibility in some cases but still fails on compliance depth; novice developers using AI assistants still omit key practices. ([CodeA11y paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.10884), [CHI 2025 ACM record](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706598.3713335))

- **A11yN** ("aligning LLMs for accessible web UI code generation") — trains/aligns a code-generating LLM via a reward function that penalizes WCAG violations, with penalty severity scaled to violation severity as scored by an accessibility testing engine (i.e., RL/DPO-style alignment against axe-core-style scoring, not just prompting).

- **A11YRepair** (arXiv 2606.21926, "knowledge-enhanced divide-and-conquer repair") and the related "Blind Edits to Verified Repair" work (arXiv 2608.24913) converge on the same architecture recommendation: **never let an LLM patch blind** — apply candidate fix → re-run an automated auditor (axe-core plus computed-style probes) → accept only if detected violations strictly decrease → otherwise roll back and reprompt with the specific violation findings as feedback. This "generate → scan → gate → loop" pattern is the clearest concrete blueprint found for how a coding-agent pipeline should structure its accessibility remediation loop.

- General 2026 framing: audits still find **>90% of public web pages contain detectable violations**; the consensus across these papers is that AI hasn't replaced accessibility specialists but "made their expertise scalable" — i.e., automation should surface candidates and human/specialist judgment should remain the gate for anything above the machine-checkable ~30–40% of criteria.

### Implication for pipeline design

- **Requirements drafting**: for each generated component, inject the machine-checkable SC list (1.1.1 presence, 1.3.1 structure, 1.4.3 contrast, 2.4.2 title, 4.1.2 name/role/value, etc.) as concrete, falsifiable generation constraints — this is what took Microsoft's eval from 12%→60%.
- **Scanning**: model the hazard taxonomy directly on axe-core's rule shape (id, impact, SC-tag, description, matcher) — it's already a proven, widely-adopted format and would let the pipeline optionally shell out to real axe-core/pa11y for the machine-checkable half rather than reinventing detection logic.
- **Judgment items**: don't let the scanner claim confidence on alt-text quality, workflow understandability, or meaningful reading order — flag these explicitly as "needs human/specialist review," mirroring CodeA11y's Reminder agent and A11y LLM Eval's finding that passing automated checks doesn't guarantee WCAG conformance.
- **Repair loop**: adopt the generate→scan→gate(strictly-decreasing-violations)→rollback-and-reprompt pattern from A11YRepair rather than one-shot fixes.</result>

## Findings Report: Accessibility as a Design Discipline (for Spec-Time Reasoning)

### 1. BBC — Accessibility Design Review (pre-code process)

BBC's practice is documented publicly at [bbc.github.io/accessibility-news-and-you](https://bbc.github.io/accessibility-news-and-you/guides/accessibility-design-review.html) (repo: [bbc/accessibility-news-and-you](https://github.com/bbc/accessibility-news-and-you/blob/master/accessibility-news-and-designers.md)) plus their formal [BBC Mobile Accessibility Standards and Guidelines](https://www.usabilityinciviclife.org/bibliography/bbc-mobile-accessibility-standards-and-guidelines-v1-0/) and a current supplier framework for accessibility consultancy/review effective Jan 2025 ([find-tender.service.gov.uk notice](https://www.find-tender.service.gov.uk/Notice/001914-2025/PDF)).

Key mechanism — a **structured design review that happens before sign-off, before any code**:
- An "accessibility champion" (any discipline, not necessarily an a11y specialist) pairs with the designer for 1–2 hours per component.
- Five-step review: visual inspection → check against key user-group considerations → compare against known best-practice references (e.g., Home Office Digital / Barclays accessibility posters) → verify user research included participants with access needs → **write out the intended screen-reader experience narrative** for the component.
- That screen-reader narrative is the deliverable that crosses the design→dev boundary — it tells developers what semantics/behavior to build to, before a line of code exists.
- Designer's own checklist requires, at design time: standard link/focus/hover states; 4.5:1 contrast (tool-checked); color-blindness simulation; explicit decision on whether icons need visually-hidden text; explicit call on heading structure/ARIA landmarks (discussed *with* developers pre-build); logical tab order; and an explicit answer to "does this degrade gracefully without JS."

**Relevance to spec-writing agents**: BBC's model proves the "screen reader experience script" is a legitimate, testable spec artifact — a designer/spec-writer states expected role/name/state announcements before implementation, which is directly falsifiable later against actual AT output.

### 2. Nielsen Norman Group — accessibility as inseparable from UX quality

Sources: [NN/g Accessibility and Inclusivity: Study Guide](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/accessibility-inclusivity-study-guide/), [NN/g accessibility topic/reports hub](https://www.nngroup.com/reports/topic/accessibility/), [Beyond Accessibility: Treating Users with Disabilities as People](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/beyond-accessibility-treating-users-with-disabilities-as-people/), [Inclusive Design: Part 2](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/inclusive-design-part-2/).

Core argument: NN/g explicitly frames **accessibility and inclusivity as branches of usability, not compliance categories** — "mindsets rather than collections of procedures, regulations, or checklists." Their stated rationale for why accessible design is just better design: features built for access needs (contrast, clear labeling, keyboard operability, predictable structure) measurably help everyone, not only disabled users — captured in their framing "accessible solutions benefit everyone." They cite population scale (an estimated 15–20% of people live with a disability, and a similar proportion is neurodiverse) as the business/design case for treating this as core UX, not edge-case handling.

Process guidance for starting-early rather than retrofitting: (a) test with actual users with disabilities early, not just automated/heuristic checks — "the only way to know if designs are accessible and usable... is to test them with this population"; (b) NN/g's "Beyond Accessibility" piece pushes teams to treat disabled users as people with goals and context, not a checkbox demographic, which argues for accessibility being part of persona/scenario work at the requirements stage, not appended later; (c) inclusive design should start at the "organizational"/planning level (Part 2, drawing on Tognazzini) — embedded in foundational project structure rather than bolted onto a finished design.

**Relevance**: Justifies a design principle for the pipeline: accessibility considerations belong in the same acceptance-criteria pass as any other UX quality bar — not a separate "a11y section" appended afterward — and that criteria should reference real assistive-tech user validation, not just automated-checker pass/fail, wherever feasible.

### 3. Other frameworks and practitioner sources

- **Microsoft Inclusive Design Toolkit** ([inclusive.microsoft.design](https://inclusive.microsoft.design/), [Inclusive 101 guidebook](https://inclusive.microsoft.design/articles/inclusive-101-guidebook)): three core principles — *recognize exclusion; learn from diversity; solve for one, extend to many*. The 2nd-edition toolkit (design-for-cognition) adds: understand user motivation/goals/tasks; assess cognitive load of the mismatch; co-create with a diverse community. Trained ~80,000 Microsoft employees and taught at 60+ universities — a widely-adopted framework for translating "who is excluded by this design decision" into an explicit design-time question, which maps well onto asking a spec-writing agent to state, per feature, who could be excluded and how the spec addresses it.

- **Heydon Pickering, Inclusive Components** ([book.inclusive-components.design](https://book.inclusive-components.design/)): philosophy is "not about wrong and right, but bad to better" — a pragmatic, non-perfectionist stance. Approach: examine one component at a time, ask who could be tripped up by it, and prefer semantic HTML + native behavior over custom JS reimplementation. Explicitly names the tension between logical document structure, visual layout, and interaction, and says compromise is inevitable but "should be an equitable sort of compromise" — useful framing for an agent judging trade-offs rather than treating a11y as pass/fail absolutist.

- **The A11Y Project checklist** ([a11yproject.com/checklist](https://www.a11yproject.com/checklist/)): built directly on WCAG as shared vocabulary, targets AA, and is explicit that "there is no such thing as 100% accessible" — the checklist is a floor for continuous improvement, not a certificate. Values noted: person-first/non-ableist language, and verifying with actual daily AT users, not just automated tooling.

- **WebAIM** ([webaim.org/standards/wcag/checklist](https://webaim.org/standards/wcag/checklist), [WCAG testability](https://webaim.org/blog/wcag-2-testability/)): translates WCAG's formal success criteria into plain-language, verifiable checks organized by the four POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust). Important structural point: **WCAG itself defines "testable" formally** — a criterion must be answerable "yes/no" by a machine, or produce ≥80% agreement among knowledgeable human evaluators (WCAG 2.x tightens this to requiring consistent results across independent testers). This is a ready-made bar for what "testable" means in an accessibility acceptance criterion.

- **GOV.UK Service Manual / GDS Way** ([gov.uk/service-manual](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/helping-people-to-use-your-service/making-your-service-accessible-an-introduction), [GDS Way accessibility](https://gds-way.digital.cabinet-office.gov.uk/manuals/accessibility.html)): explicit rule that "accessibility cannot be achieved by adding final touches — it must be considered at all stages," and assigns accessibility ownership by role (content/interaction designers avoid inaccessible patterns, researchers test for it, delivery managers ensure it's considered from the start) — a concrete distribution-of-responsibility model rather than leaving it to one specialist.

### 4. Writing testable, falsifiable accessibility acceptance criteria — the key finding

The most directly applicable pattern is **Deque's "a11yAC" (Accessibility Acceptance Criteria)**, part of their "a11yBID" (Accessibility Behavior-Informed Development) methodology — [Deque: Collaborative planning, the forgotten step of accessible development](https://www.deque.com/blog/collaborative-planning-the-forgotten-step-of-accessible-development/). This is the closest real-world analog to what this pipeline needs:

- a11yAC are written in **Gherkin Given-When-Then** form, same as functional acceptance criteria, and live in the same user story — not a separate a11y appendix.
- Concrete example given:
  > Given I am a blind screen reader user, and I have submitted the form, and a loading spinner is visible as I await a response from the server, When I navigate to the loading spinner image, Then I hear the image role, and I hear the alt text as "loading."
- Explicit design rule: a11yAC should be **agnostic to specific assistive-tech key commands** and instead state the expected *semantics* (role, state, property/name) — i.e., criteria are written against the accessibility-tree contract, not against "press NVDA+X and hear Y," which keeps them stable across AT implementations while remaining falsifiable.
- Process: a "**11y Amigos**" session (analyst/story-writer + developer + tester + designer — a variant of BDD's "three amigos") discovers and documents a11yAC **before development starts**, explicitly because "no single person is expected to know enough about all aspects of accessibility to write quality requirements" — knowledge is distributed across roles rather than assumed to live in one person's head.
- Stated downstream payoff: developers read a11yAC to know what to build and self-test; testers read them to know what to verify; product owners use them as the bar for accepting the story; future maintainers use them to understand why an accessibility-driven implementation choice was made (preventing accidental regression).
- Note: design-specific requirements (contrast, color, spacing) are captured in the visual design artifact itself, not in a11yAC — a11yAC exist specifically to cover what a static visual design cannot express: assistive-technology behavior, states, and announcements.

Complementary: **Deque also runs accessibility heuristic evaluations at the design phase itself** ([Supporting Design: Accessibility Heuristics Evaluation](https://www.deque.com/blog/supporting-the-design-phase-with-accessibility-heuristics-evaluations/)), reinforcing that a11y review belongs at the design/spec review gate, not only at code review.

**WCAG's formal testability bar** (from WebAIM) gives a crisp definition an agent can apply when judging whether a proposed criterion is "testable": it must be answerable objectively (automatable) or reach high inter-rater agreement among evaluators — this is a good litmus test to reject vague criteria like "must be accessible" or "should work with screen readers" in favor of Given-When-Then statements naming a specific role/state/name/behavior.

---

### Synthesis for the pipeline's spec-drafting agents

1. **Treat accessibility acceptance criteria as first-class criteria in the same list as functional ones**, written Given-When-Then, naming assistive-technology-observable semantics (role, name, state, announced text, focus behavior) rather than visual description or vague compliance language — directly modeled on Deque's a11yAC pattern and WCAG's testability bar.
2. **Require an explicit exclusion/persona pass at spec time** ("who could be excluded by this interaction and how does the spec address it") — Microsoft's "recognize exclusion / solve for one, extend to many" gives a concrete prompt shape for this.
3. **Require a stated assistive-tech experience narrative for any new interactive component**, before implementation — BBC's practice of writing the intended screen-reader experience as a design deliverable is a template for a criterion category: "expected AT narrative."
4. **Reject "must be accessible"-style criteria outright** as a spec smell — the whole body of sources (WCAG testability rule, Deque's a11yAC, NN/g's rejection of "checklist" thinking) converges on requiring criteria phrased as falsifiable propositions with a stated verification method (automatable check, or a named evaluator procedure with expected agreement).
5. **Frame accessibility judgment as pragmatic and comparative ("bad to better"), not pass/fail perfectionist** — Heydon Pickering's and A11Y Project's shared stance — useful for an adversarial gate agent (like axiom or canon's auditor) that should flag missing/ambiguous a11y criteria as blockers but not demand an unattainable "100% accessible" bar.
6. **Assign accessibility review to a broadened cast, not a single specialist** — GOV.UK's per-role responsibility model and Deque's "a11y Amigos" both argue against having accessibility live only in one gate agent's judgment; worth reflecting in how the pipeline distributes accessibility-checking responsibility across draft-spec, audit-spec, and gate-spec rather than concentrating it in one late step.</result>

- **Microsoft Inclusive Design Toolkit** ([inclusive.microsoft.design](https://inclusive.microsoft.design/), [Inclusive 101 guidebook](https://inclusive.microsoft.design/articles/inclusive-101-guidebook)): three core principles — *recognize exclusion; learn from diversity; solve for one, extend to many*. The 2nd-edition toolkit (design-for-cognition) adds: understand user motivation/goals/tasks; assess cognitive load of the mismatch; co-create with a diverse community. Trained ~80,000 Microsoft employees and taught at 60+ universities — a widely-adopted framework for translating "who is excluded by this design decision" into an explicit design-time question, which maps well onto asking a spec-writing agent to state, per feature, who could be excluded and how the spec addresses it.

- **Heydon Pickering, Inclusive Components** ([book.inclusive-components.design](https://book.inclusive-components.design/)): philosophy is "not about wrong and right, but bad to better" — a pragmatic, non-perfectionist stance. Approach: examine one component at a time, ask who could be tripped up by it, and prefer semantic HTML + native behavior over custom JS reimplementation. Explicitly names the tension between logical document structure, visual layout, and interaction, and says compromise is inevitable but "should be an equitable sort of compromise" — useful framing for an agent judging trade-offs rather than treating a11y as pass/fail absolutist.

- **The A11Y Project checklist** ([a11yproject.com/checklist](https://www.a11yproject.com/checklist/)): built directly on WCAG as shared vocabulary, targets AA, and is explicit that "there is no such thing as 100% accessible" — the checklist is a floor for continuous improvement, not a certificate. Values noted: person-first/non-ableist language, and verifying with actual daily AT users, not just automated tooling.

- **WebAIM** ([webaim.org/standards/wcag/checklist](https://webaim.org/standards/wcag/checklist), [WCAG testability](https://webaim.org/blog/wcag-2-testability/)): translates WCAG's formal success criteria into plain-language, verifiable checks organized by the four POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust). Important structural point: **WCAG itself defines "testable" formally** — a criterion must be answerable "yes/no" by a machine, or produce ≥80% agreement among knowledgeable human evaluators (WCAG 2.x tightens this to requiring consistent results across independent testers). This is a ready-made bar for what "testable" means in an accessibility acceptance criterion.

- **GOV.UK Service Manual / GDS Way** ([gov.uk/service-manual](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/helping-people-to-use-your-service/making-your-service-accessible-an-introduction), [GDS Way accessibility](https://gds-way.digital.cabinet-office.gov.uk/manuals/accessibility.html)): explicit rule that "accessibility cannot be achieved by adding final touches — it must be considered at all stages," and assigns accessibility ownership by role (content/interaction designers avoid inaccessible patterns, researchers test for it, delivery managers ensure it's considered from the start) — a concrete distribution-of-responsibility model rather than leaving it to one specialist.

### 4. Writing testable, falsifiable accessibility acceptance criteria — the key finding

The most directly applicable pattern is **Deque's "a11yAC" (Accessibility Acceptance Criteria)**, part of their "a11yBID" (Accessibility Behavior-Informed Development) methodology — [Deque: Collaborative planning, the forgotten step of accessible development](https://www.deque.com/blog/collaborative-planning-the-forgotten-step-of-accessible-development/). This is the closest real-world analog to what this pipeline needs:

- a11yAC are written in **Gherkin Given-When-Then** form, same as functional acceptance criteria, and live in the same user story — not a separate a11y appendix.
- Concrete example given:
  > Given I am a blind screen reader user, and I have submitted the form, and a loading spinner is visible as I await a response from the server, When I navigate to the loading spinner image, Then I hear the image role, and I hear the alt text as "loading."
- Explicit design rule: a11yAC should be **agnostic to specific assistive-tech key commands** and instead state the expected *semantics* (role, state, property/name) — i.e., criteria are written against the accessibility-tree contract, not against "press NVDA+X and hear Y," which keeps them stable across AT implementations while remaining falsifiable.
- Process: a "**11y Amigos**" session (analyst/story-writer + developer + tester + designer — a variant of BDD's "three amigos") discovers and documents a11yAC **before development starts**, explicitly because "no single person is expected to know enough about all aspects of accessibility to write quality requirements" — knowledge is distributed across roles rather than assumed to live in one person's head.
- Stated downstream payoff: developers read a11yAC to know what to build and self-test; testers read them to know what to verify; product owners use them as the bar for accepting the story; future maintainers use them to understand why an accessibility-driven implementation choice was made (preventing accidental regression).
- Note: design-specific requirements (contrast, color, spacing) are captured in the visual design artifact itself, not in a11yAC — a11yAC exist specifically to cover what a static visual design cannot express: assistive-technology behavior, states, and announcements.

Complementary: **Deque also runs accessibility heuristic evaluations at the design phase itself** ([Supporting Design: Accessibility Heuristics Evaluation](https://www.deque.com/blog/supporting-the-design-phase-with-accessibility-heuristics-evaluations/)), reinforcing that a11y review belongs at the design/spec review gate, not only at code review.

**WCAG's formal testability bar** (from WebAIM) gives a crisp definition an agent can apply when judging whether a proposed criterion is "testable": it must be answerable objectively (automatable) or reach high inter-rater agreement among evaluators — this is a good litmus test to reject vague criteria like "must be accessible" or "should work with screen readers" in favor of Given-When-Then statements naming a specific role/state/name/behavior.

---

### Synthesis for the pipeline's spec-drafting agents

1. **Treat accessibility acceptance criteria as first-class criteria in the same list as functional ones**, written Given-When-Then, naming assistive-technology-observable semantics (role, name, state, announced text, focus behavior) rather than visual description or vague compliance language — directly modeled on Deque's a11yAC pattern and WCAG's testability bar.
2. **Require an explicit exclusion/persona pass at spec time** ("who could be excluded by this interaction and how does the spec address it") — Microsoft's "recognize exclusion / solve for one, extend to many" gives a concrete prompt shape for this.
3. **Require a stated assistive-tech experience narrative for any new interactive component**, before implementation — BBC's practice of writing the intended screen-reader experience as a design deliverable is a template for a criterion category: "expected AT narrative."
4. **Reject "must be accessible"-style criteria outright** as a spec smell — the whole body of sources (WCAG testability rule, Deque's a11yAC, NN/g's rejection of "checklist" thinking) converges on requiring criteria phrased as falsifiable propositions with a stated verification method (automatable check, or a named evaluator procedure with expected agreement).
5. **Frame accessibility judgment as pragmatic and comparative ("bad to better"), not pass/fail perfectionist** — Heydon Pickering's and A11Y Project's shared stance — useful for an adversarial gate agent (like axiom or canon's auditor) that should flag missing/ambiguous a11y criteria as blockers but not demand an unattainable "100% accessible" bar.
6. **Assign accessibility review to a broadened cast, not a single specialist** — GOV.UK's per-role responsibility model and Deque's "a11y Amigos" both argue against having accessibility live only in one gate agent's judgment; worth reflecting in how the pipeline distributes accessibility-checking responsibility across draft-spec, audit-spec, and gate-spec rather than concentrating it in one late step.</result>

<result># Research Report: CLI/Terminal Accessibility

**Question:** What does accessibility for command-line interfaces and terminal applications require, in the absence of a formal standard — and what would a WCAG-style set of checkable rules for terminals look like, organized by topic, drawing on clig.dev, NO_COLOR/FORCE_COLOR, GitHub's 2025 CLI accessibility work, the 2021 CHI paper, Seirdy/AFixt checklists, PatternFly's CLI handbook, and known TUI framework gaps (Textual/Ratatui/Bubble Tea)?

## Headline Finding: No WCAG Equivalent Exists

There is no ratified, industry-standard accessibility specification for CLIs or terminal applications, comparable to WCAG for the web. There is no standardized "accessibility tree" analogous to the DOM/ARIA that assistive technology can query — a terminal is, structurally, an unstructured stream of text (confirmed, CHI '21 paper, dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3411764.3445544). What exists instead is a patchwork: one peer-reviewed study (CHI 2021), one long-standing community output-style guide that is *not* accessibility-focused (clig.dev), a handful of independent practitioner checklists (Seirdy, AFixt), one vendor design-system handbook (PatternFly), and post-hoc engineering blog posts from vendors who hit real accessibility bugs and fixed them (GitHub, 2025). Confidence in this landscape claim: likely (AFixt, https://afixt.com/accessible-by-design-improving-command-line-interfaces-for-all-users/, is the only source stating the absence explicitly; corroborated by the CHI paper's framing and the absence of any accessibility section in clig.dev).

Below, findings are organized into six topic areas, each expressed as a checkable rule set. Every rule cites its source and carries the confidence label from the underlying finding (confirmed / likely / assumed).

---

## Topic 1: Output Streams, Machine-Readability & Exit Codes

The foundational layer: before a screen reader can do anything useful with CLI output, the program must separate what's meant to be read from what's meant to be parsed.

- **1.1 (confirmed)** Primary output goes to stdout; diagnostics/logs go to stderr. Source: clig.dev.
- **1.2 (confirmed)** Return zero exit code on success, non-zero on failure, so scripted/AT-mediated workflows can branch reliably. Source: clig.dev.
- **1.3 (likely)** A more granular exit-code convention (sysexits.h, BSD-origin, adopted by some GNU/Linux libcs) exists beyond POSIX's simple binary model, but is not universally followed — treat as an enhancement, not a baseline requirement. Source: https://www.gsp.com/cgi-bin/man.cgi?section=3&topic=sysexits.
- **1.4 (confirmed)** Provide machine-readable output modes: `--json` for structured output, `--plain` for tabular text usable with grep/awk. Source: clig.dev.
- **1.5 (confirmed)** Use TTY-ness as the default heuristic for "is a human or a machine consuming this stream" — but this heuristic is orthogonal to accessibility, since a screen-reader user's session still presents as a TTY. ## Topic 2: Color

- **2.1 (confirmed)** Disable color automatically when stdout is not an interactive terminal. Source: clig.dev.
- **2.2 (confirmed)** Honor `NO_COLOR`: if the environment variable is present and non-empty (regardless of value), suppress all ANSI color, with no per-program opt-out. Source: https://no-color.org/.
- **2.3 (confirmed)** Support a `FORCE_COLOR` override (numeric levels 0-3) for cases where color should be forced even though auto-detection would disable it. Source: https://github.com/chalk/supports-color. Note: unlike NO_COLOR, this is a library convention (chalk/supports-color), not a ratified cross-ecosystem standard — likely confidence on that distinction (https://force-color.org/).
- **2.4 (confirmed)** Never convey meaning by color alone; pair color with a text label (e.g., "Success"/"Error"). Source: PatternFly CLI handbook, https://www.patternfly.org/content-design/writing-guides/cli-handbook/.
- **2.5 (confirmed)** When color is used, constrain it to the 16-color (4-bit) ANSI palette, because that is the only palette range most terminal emulators let users remap for contrast/colorblindness — 24-bit "true color" defeats user-level remapping. Source: GitHub engineering blog, https://github.blog/engineering/user-experience/building-a-more-accessible-github-cli/.
- **2.6 (confirmed)** Support `--color=always|never|auto` as an explicit user-facing override, independent of NO_COLOR/FORCE_COLOR env vars. Source: Seirdy, https://seirdy.one/posts/2022/06/10/cli-best-practices/.
- **2.7 (confirmed)** Treat `TERM=dumb` as a signal to strip all formatting, not just color. Source: AFixt.

## Topic 3: Animation, Spinners & Progress Indication

This is the area with the strongest, most repeated confirmed failure pattern across independent vendors.

- **3.1 (confirmed)** Suppress animations entirely when stdout is not an interactive terminal. Source: clig.dev.
- **3.2 (confirmed)** Animated spinners are "extremely problematic for screen readers" in nearly all cases — screen readers either vocalize the underlying Unicode/braille glyphs literally, or the rapid redraw causes the AT to skip/freeze on lines. Source: Seirdy; corroborated independently by GitHub CLI's own bug fix (below) and Google Cloud's gdcloud CLI accessibility docs (likely confidence on the Google corroboration).
- **3.3 (confirmed)** Real-world confirmed regressions consistent with 3.2: GitHub CLI's original spinner used braille-pattern Unicode characters intended for physical Braille displays, not animation, and screen readers misread them — GitHub replaced it with a static text progress indicator as part of its accessibility mode. Source: GitHub engineering blog.
- **3.4 (confirmed)** Anthropic's Claude Code has an open issue (#11002) where NVDA freezes during token-streaming/spinner updates, requiring users to restart the screen reader multiple times per session — described by affected users as making the tool "largely unusable" for accessibility-focused Windows users. Source: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/11002.
- **3.5 (confirmed)** GitHub Copilot CLI shipped `--screen-reader` and `--no-banner` flags specifically to suppress decorative ASCII art (read character-by-character by AT) and animated elements. Source: GitHub accessibility docs, https://accessibility.github.com/documentation/guide/cli/.
- **3.6 (confirmed)** Counter-example / live bug even after a fix was shipped: GitHub Copilot CLI's screen-reader mode has a reported regression where a percentage status-bar value is re-announced on every keypress instead of echoing typed characters, making the prompt effectively unusable — evidence that shipping an accessibility flag is not sufficient; it must be tested against real interaction sequences. Source: https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/issues/1642.
- **3.7 (confirmed)** Rule derived from 3.1–3.6: ship an explicit, discoverable flag (`--no-animation`, `--static-output`, `--screen-reader`) that replaces all dynamic redraw with static, line-appended status text — do not rely on TTY-detection alone (see 1.5), since a screen-reader session is still a TTY. Source: synthesis of AFixt, GitHub, Seirdy.

**Contradiction to surface:** the CHI paper (3-and-4-topic source) found users "strongly preferred bare mode free of decoration/color/animation" (likely, paraphrase) — this is consistent with 3.1–3.7, so no real contradiction here; treat this as convergent confirmation across a peer-reviewed source and multiple vendor engineering blogs, which is a genuine pattern, not coincidence.

## Topic 4: Structural Semantics — Text Alternatives, Escape Codes, Decoration

- **4.1 (confirmed)** CLIs are fundamentally "unstructured text interfaces" with no accessibility-tree equivalent to HTML/DOM — this is the structural root cause behind most of the other findings in this report, not a bug in any one tool. Source: CHI '21 paper (abstract-level access only — full text was inaccessible, 403 both attempts, so treat any paraphrased detail beyond the abstract as likely, not confirmed).
- **4.2 (confirmed)** Provide text alternatives for ASCII art / decorative logos, analogous to WCAG 1.1.1, and make them opt-in only via flags (`--fancy`, `--logo`) rather than default-on. Source: AFixt.
- **4.3 (likely)** Box-drawing/border characters get announced verbosely and repeatedly by screen readers (e.g., "box drawing light horizontal" read out on every character) — reported in Claude Code issue #247, but sourced via a search summary rather than the primary issue text, so kept at likely rather than confirmed.
- **4.4 (likely)** Raw ANSI escape sequences, when not stripped or interpreted, are read aloud as literal byte sequences by screen readers — reported as a recurring, structurally-rooted failure across multiple independently-reported cases (Copilot CLI, Claude Code, general tooling), not one isolated bug. Source: https://blog.safia.rocks/2025/12/22/ansi-codes/ (via search summary).
- **4.5 (confirmed)** Prefer plain structured output — headings, bullets, clear separators — that a screen reader can parse linearly, over dense ASCII tables or "walls of text." Source: PatternFly CLI handbook.
- **4.6 (confirmed)** Man pages have a standardized, predictable, searchable format that screen-reader users have built specialized navigation scripts around — this is cited as a positive existing pattern worth preserving/extending, not a gap. Source: Seirdy.

## Topic 5: TUI Frameworks & Terminal Emulators — The Structural Regression

This is the most important and counter-intuitive pattern in the whole research set, and the one most likely to surprise a spec writer who assumes "newer framework = more accessible."

- **5.1 (confirmed)** Bubble Tea (Charm, Go) has an open, unresolved issue asking whether screen-reader accessibility is on the roadmap; the maintainers have made no roadmap commitment. The core barrier stated is that TUI text has no structural markup for screen readers to parse. Source: https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/issues/780.
- **5.2 (confirmed)** Proposed (not implemented) workaround for Bubble Tea: a secondary structured-text buffer maintained in parallel to the visual TUI for screen readers, or a `--web` flag serving an HTML view instead. Source: same issue.
- **5.3 (likely)** Charm's `huh?` form/prompt library has a first-class accessible mode, distinguishing it from Bubble Tea itself — the accessibility gap is specific to the full-screen TUI redraw model, not to Charm's tooling in general.
- **5.4 (assumed)** Ratatui (Rust) has no confirmed dedicated accessibility feature. A `-sr`/screenreader flag has been proposed elsewhere but is not confirmed implemented in Ratatui itself. Ratatui issue #985 (confirmed) documents that rendered text cannot even be copied from the terminal, independently blocking AT text-selection workflows regardless of screen-reader support. Source: https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/issues/985.
- **5.5 (likely)** Textual (Python) markets monochrome mode, high-contrast themes, and colorblind themes as accessibility features, but full screen-reader integration for blind users is explicitly described by the project as still planned, not shipped — Textual is the most accessibility-forward of the three frameworks surveyed and still has not shipped the core capability (screen-reader support). Source: textual.textualize.io (via search synthesis).
- **5.6 (likely)** curses/ncurses-based interfaces are broadly considered inaccessible by design — raw character rendering for line-drawing, checkboxes, and color-based focus indication exposes no semantic structure. This is treated as a structural limitation of the terminal I/O model itself, not a fixable library bug. Source: HN discussion, urwid.org docs.

Reported symptoms: screen readers reading "random bits of conversation mixed with timer updates," multi-second paste-input lag, and one claimed case of NVDA instability from per-keystroke layout recalculation. The author is a Speakup (Linux console screen reader) user writing from personal experience, with no stated professional/research credentials — this is an opinion/experience post, not peer-reviewed, and the NVDA-crash claim specifically is the author's personal assertion, not independently corroborated. Source: blindcomputing.org, https://blindcomputing.org/linux/state-of-cli-accessibility/.
- **5.9 (likely)** tmux/screen vertical pane splitting is itself an accessibility failure mode independent of terminal emulator: the screen reader reads text from both panes at the cursor's row, merging unrelated content — unlike a GUI split widget, which exposes panes as separate accessible regions. Source: synthesis citing xogium.me content.
- **5.10 (confirmed)** At the OS/console level (distinct from terminal emulators), Speakup (kernel-module console screen reader) + espeak works well at the raw TTY level; Fenrir is a newer, actively-developed userspace alternative with better highlight tracking and scripting. Confidence: medium — this rests on convergent likely/assumed findings (5.1–5.7) rather than a single confirmed comparative study, but the convergence across four independent frameworks and one experience report is itself meaningful signal.

- **6.4 (confirmed)** GitHub's 2025 accessibility work (dated May 2025) — screen-reader mode, colorblind-friendly theme picker, keyboard-first navigation, layouts adapted for narrower terminal windows — is one of the most concrete, recent, real-world shipped artifacts found in this research and the closest thing to a "reference implementation" currently available. A tangential paper on programming education for blind/low-vision users exists but is not CLI-accessibility-specific. This absence itself is a finding worth surfacing to a spec writer: there is no active research community to consult for edge cases, only after-the-fact vendor postmortems.

## Synthesis: What "Consensus Best Practice" Actually Looks Like

No single source above is authoritative on its own. But triangulating the confirmed findings across clig.dev (general CLI conventions), the CHI 2021 paper (the only peer-reviewed empirical study), GitHub's 2025 shipped features (the only large-scale production accessibility effort), and the independent checklists (Seirdy, AFixt, PatternFly) — which converge independently, not by citing each other — produces a stable, non-contradictory core:

1. Detect non-interactive/AT contexts and default to plain, static, non-color, non-animated, structured text output — but don't rely on TTY-detection alone; ship an explicit opt-in/opt-out flag, because a screen-reader session still looks like a TTY.
2. Never encode meaning in color or animation alone; always pair with text.
3. Respect NO_COLOR/FORCE_COLOR/`--color=` as three converging but distinct control surfaces (env-var convention, library convention, and explicit CLI flag respectively) — support all three, since none subsumes the other in practice.
4. Provide `--json`/`--plain` for machine consumption, which doubles as the accessibility workaround CHI-paper participants already use.
5. Treat full-screen, canvas-redrawing TUI frameworks as a currently-unsolved accessibility risk, not a UX upgrade — this is the finding most likely to be missed by a spec writer defaulting to "use a modern TUI framework because it looks nicer."
6. Test with actual screen readers (or at minimum espeak-ng) before shipping, because accessibility bugs in this space are behavioral/interactive (per-keystroke re-announcement, spinner glyph misreads) and are not caught by static review.

There is no explicit contradiction between confirmed and assumed findings that requires surfacing as an either/or choice — the assumed/likely findings (Topic 5 TUI framework gaps, the ANSI-escape-code pattern, the CHI-workaround inference) are all directionally consistent with the confirmed findings; they extend the picture rather than opposing it. The one place genuine tension exists is intuition vs. evidence: the intuitive assumption that newer, more polished TUI frameworks are more accessible is contradicted by every framework-specific finding gathered (5.1–5.7). That should be stated to the spec writer explicitly, since it cuts against a natural default choice.

## Recommendation

Adopt the six-topic rule set above as the working "terminal accessibility baseline" in place of a formal standard, with explicit sourcing and confidence labels retained per rule (do not present them as equal-confidence WCAG-style success criteria — the confidence label is load-bearing information, not metadata). Concretely: (a) default all new CLI/TUI work to Topic 1–4's plain/static/structured baseline; (b) treat any full-screen TUI framework (Bubble Tea, Ratatui, Textual, Ink, curses) as accessibility-risk-bearing by default and require an explicit static/linear fallback mode before shipping, per Topic 5; (c) require espeak-ng or real screen-reader testing as a release gate per Topic 6, since the confirmed regressions (GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code) all shipped past normal review and were caught only by affected users in production. Rationale: this ordering follows the confidence gradient in the evidence — rules 1–4 rest on confirmed, multiply-corroborated sources; rule (b) rests on convergent likely/assumed findings across independent frameworks, which is weaker per-source but strong in aggregate; rule (c) is justified by the fact that every confirmed production failure found in this research (3.3, 3.4, 3.6) was interactive/behavioral and would not have been caught by static code review alone.

**Confidence: medium.** High confidence in the individual confirmed findings and in the absence of a formal standard; medium (not high) on the overall recommendation because it synthesizes across sources of uneven rigor (one peer-reviewed paper whose full text was unreachable, several vendor blogs, and independent practitioner posts), and because the TUI-framework-regression pattern (Topic 5), while convergent, rests on likely/assumed evidence rather than a single confirmed comparative study.

## Open Questions

- IF the CHI '21 paper's full text (currently inaccessible, 403 both attempts) contains a formal taxonomy or severity ranking of CLI accessibility failures THEN the six-topic organization above should be revised to match that taxonomy rather than this synthesis's inferred grouping, and rules currently marked "likely" via secondary paraphrase (1.2 CHI-paraphrase items, 4.1 detail beyond the abstract) should be re-confidence-rated against the primary source.
- IF Textual, Ratatui, or Bubble Tea ship confirmed, tested screen-reader support after this research's cutoff THEN the Topic 5 recommendation (avoid full-screen TUI frameworks by default) should be narrowed to name only the frameworks still lacking support, rather than applying blanket caution to the category.
- IF the Claude Code Issue #247 claim (box-drawing characters read verbosely) is confirmed from the primary issue text rather than a search summary THEN it should be promoted from likely to confirmed and can be cited standalone rather than only in aggregate with the ANSI-escape-code pattern.
- IF a target user population is predominantly using GTK-based terminal emulators (gnome-terminal, xfce4-terminal, mate-terminal) rather than XTerm/urxvt/st/Konsole THEN the terminal-emulator-choice finding (5.8) becomes a non-issue for that population and the spec's scope can drop terminal-emulator compatibility as a requirement — but this should be verified against actual user telemetry, not assumed.
- IF the xogium.me "text mode lie" article's core claim (VT100 scrolling-region-based CLIs are more accessible than canvas-redrawing TUIs) is independently confirmed by a second source THEN the Topic 5 recommendation should be strengthened from "treat as risk-bearing, require fallback" to "avoid outright, prefer scrolling-region-based rendering by default."
