- **5.1 (confirmed)** Bubble Tea (Charm, Go) has an open, unresolved issue asking whether screen-reader accessibility is on the roadmap; the maintainers have made no roadmap commitment. The core barrier stated is that TUI text has no structural markup for screen readers to parse. Source: https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea/issues/780.
- **5.2 (confirmed)** Proposed (not implemented) workaround for Bubble Tea: a secondary structured-text buffer maintained in parallel to the visual TUI for screen readers, or a `--web` flag serving an HTML view instead. Source: same issue.
- **5.3 (likely)** Charm's `huh?` form/prompt library has a first-class accessible mode, distinguishing it from Bubble Tea itself — the accessibility gap is specific to the full-screen TUI redraw model, not to Charm's tooling in general.
- **5.4 (assumed)** Ratatui (Rust) has no confirmed dedicated accessibility feature. A `-sr`/screenreader flag has been proposed elsewhere but is not confirmed implemented in Ratatui itself. Ratatui issue #985 (confirmed) documents that rendered text cannot even be copied from the terminal, independently blocking AT text-selection workflows regardless of screen-reader support. Source: https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui/issues/985.
- **5.5 (likely)** Textual (Python) markets monochrome mode, high-contrast themes, and colorblind themes as accessibility features, but full screen-reader integration for blind users is explicitly described by the project as still planned, not shipped — Textual is the most accessibility-forward of the three frameworks surveyed and still has not shipped the core capability (screen-reader support). Source: textual.textualize.io (via search synthesis).
- **5.6 (likely)** curses/ncurses-based interfaces are broadly considered inaccessible by design — raw character rendering for line-drawing, checkboxes, and color-based focus indication exposes no semantic structure. This is treated as a structural limitation of the terminal I/O model itself, not a fixable library bug. Source: HN discussion, urwid.org docs.
- **5.7 (confirmed, article's claim — underlying crash claim unverified)** A blog post ("The text mode lie") argues that modern declarative TUI frameworks (Ink, Bubble Tea, tcell) can be *worse* for screen readers than old simple scrollback CLIs, because they redraw/diff the whole screen like a canvas instead of using VT100 scrolling regions. Reported symptoms: screen readers reading "random bits of conversation mixed with timer updates," multi-second paste-input lag, and one claimed case of NVDA instability from per-keystroke layout recalculation. The author is a Speakup (Linux console screen reader) user writing from personal experience, with no stated professional/research credentials — this is an opinion/experience post, not peer-reviewed, and the NVDA-crash claim specifically is the author's personal assertion, not independently corroborated. Treat 5.7 as a real, plausible pattern worth designing against, but do not cite it with the same weight as the CHI paper.
- **5.8 (confirmed)** Terminal emulator choice materially affects accessibility independent of the application running inside it: GTK-based terminals (xfce4-terminal, mate-terminal, gnome-terminal) are fully accessible; Terminator is accessible with caveats (vertical split panes don't read multiple lines correctly); XTerm, urxvt, st (suckless), and Qt-based Konsole are NOT accessible. Source: blindcomputing.org, https://blindcomputing.org/linux/state-of-cli-accessibility/.
- **5.9 (likely)** tmux/screen vertical pane splitting is itself an accessibility failure mode independent of terminal emulator: the screen reader reads text from both panes at the cursor's row, merging unrelated content — unlike a GUI split widget, which exposes panes as separate accessible regions. Source: synthesis citing xogium.me content.
- **5.10 (confirmed)** At the OS/console level (distinct from terminal emulators), Speakup (kernel-module console screen reader) + espeak works well at the raw TTY level; Fenrir is a newer, actively-developed userspace alternative with better highlight tracking and scripting. Debian and Arch offer pre-configured accessible installs. Source: blindcomputing.org.

**Rule derived from Topic 5 (the single most spec-relevant takeaway of this report):** a TUI framework choice is itself an accessibility decision, not a neutral implementation detail. Full-screen, canvas-redrawing frameworks (Bubble Tea, Ratatui, Textual, Ink) are, at the time of this research, all either unshipped or actively reported as regressions on screen-reader accessibility. A plain, linear, append-only scrollback interface using stdout/stderr discipline (Topic 1) plus a `--screen-reader`-style static-text mode (Topic 3) is currently the *more* accessible choice than a modern TUI, not the less sophisticated one. Confidence: medium — this rests on convergent likely/assumed findings (5.1–5.7) rather than a single confirmed comparative study, but the convergence across four independent frameworks and one experience report is itself meaningful signal.

---

## Topic 6: Explicit Accessibility Modes, Testing & Documentation

- **6.1 (confirmed)** GitHub CLI shipped a formal `gh a11y` accessibility mode (v2.72.0+) covering prompts, progress indicators, and color; it replaced its prompt library with charmbracelet/huh for screen-reader-compatible prompts. Source: GitHub engineering blog.
- **6.2 (confirmed)** GitHub's guidance recommends numbered-list selection instead of arrow-key navigation for screen-reader users, and recommends Windows Terminal's "Mark Mode" for reviewing scrolled output line by line. Source: https://accessibility.github.com/documentation/guide/cli/.
- **6.3 (confirmed)** GitHub's own stated conclusion: no single universally "accessible" CLI output format exists; individual customization (explicit flags, user-level config) is necessary rather than a single default that works for everyone. Source: same.
- **6.4 (confirmed)** GitHub's 2025 accessibility work (dated May 2025) — screen-reader mode, colorblind-friendly theme picker, keyboard-first navigation, layouts adapted for narrower terminal windows — is one of the most concrete, recent, real-world shipped artifacts found in this research and the closest thing to a "reference implementation" currently available. Source: https://github.blog/changelog/2025-05-01-improved-accessibility-features-in-github-cli/, https://github.blog/open-source/building-githubs-next-chapter-in-accessibility/.
- **6.5 (confirmed)** Mandate testing with real screen readers and colorblind simulators before release, not just automated linting. Source: PatternFly CLI handbook.
- **6.6 (confirmed)** Concrete, cheap test method: pipe your CLI's output through `espeak-ng` and listen to it, as a low-cost proxy for full screen-reader testing. Source: Seirdy.
- **6.7 (confirmed)** Document accessibility-relevant flags prominently in `--help` output, not buried in a separate accessibility doc a user has to already know exists. Source: AFixt.
- **6.8 (assumed)** There is no dedicated, sustained conference-talk circuit specific to CLI/terminal accessibility from 2023–2026; the field runs on one peer-reviewed paper (2021), scattered independent blog posts of varying rigor, and vendor engineering blogs describing shipped fixes after the fact rather than proactive research. A tangential paper on programming education for blind/low-vision users exists but is not CLI-accessibility-specific. This absence itself is a finding worth surfacing to a spec writer: there is no active research community to consult for edge cases, only after-the-fact vendor postmortems.

---

## Synthesis: What "Consensus Best Practice" Actually Looks Like

No single source above is authoritative on its own. But triangulating the confirmed findings across clig.dev (general CLI conventions), the CHI 2021 paper (the only peer-reviewed empirical study), GitHub's 2025 shipped features (the only large-scale production accessibility effort), and the independent checklists (Seirdy, AFixt, PatternFly) — which converge independently, not by citing each other — produces a stable, non-contradictory core:

1. Detect non-interactive/AT contexts and default to plain, static, non-color, non-animated, structured text output — but don't rely on TTY-detection alone; ship an explicit opt-in/opt-out flag, because a screen-reader session still looks like a TTY.
2. Never encode meaning in color or animation alone; always pair with text.
3. Respect NO_COLOR/FORCE_COLOR/`--color=` as three converging but distinct control surfaces (env-var convention, library convention, and explicit CLI flag respectively) — support all three, since none subsumes the other in practice.
4. Provide `--json`/`--plain` for machine consumption, which doubles as the accessibility workaround CHI-paper participants already use.
5. Treat full-screen, canvas-redrawing TUI frameworks as a currently-unsolved accessibility risk, not a UX upgrade — this is the finding most likely to be missed by a spec writer defaulting to "use a modern TUI framework because it looks nicer."
6. Test with actual screen readers (or at minimum espeak-ng) before shipping, because accessibility bugs in this space are behavioral/interactive (per-keystroke re-announcement, spinner glyph misreads) and are not caught by static review.

There is no explicit contradiction between confirmed and assumed findings that requires surfacing as an either/or choice — the assumed/likely findings (Topic 5 TUI framework gaps, the ANSI-escape-code pattern, the CHI-workaround inference) are all directionally consistent with the confirmed findings; they extend the picture rather than opposing it. The one place genuine tension exists is intuition vs. evidence: the intuitive assumption that newer, more polished TUI frameworks are more accessible is contradicted by every framework-specific finding gathered (5.1–5.7). That should be stated to the spec writer explicitly, since it cuts against a natural default choice.

## Recommendation

Adopt the six-topic rule set above as the working "terminal accessibility baseline" in place of a formal standard, with explicit sourcing and confidence labels retained per rule (do not present them as equal-confidence WCAG-style success criteria — the confidence label is load-bearing information, not metadata). Concretely: (a) default all new CLI/TUI work to Topic 1–4's plain/static/structured baseline; (b) treat any full-screen TUI framework (Bubble Tea, Ratatui, Textual, Ink, curses) as accessibility-risk-bearing by default and require an explicit static/linear fallback mode before shipping, per Topic 5; (c) require espeak-ng or real screen-reader testing as a release gate per Topic 6, since the confirmed regressions (GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code) all shipped past normal review and were caught only by affected users in production. Rationale: this ordering follows the confidence gradient in the evidence — rules 1–4 rest on confirmed, multiply-corroborated sources; rule (b) rests on convergent likely/assumed findings across independent frameworks, which is weaker per-source but strong in aggregate; rule (c) is justified by the fact that every confirmed production failure found in this research (3.3, 3.4, 3.6) was interactive/behavioral and would not have been caught by static code review alone.

**Confidence: medium.** High confidence in the individual confirmed findings and in the absence of a formal standard; medium (not high) on the overall recommendation because it synthesizes across sources of uneven rigor (one peer-reviewed paper whose full text was unreachable, several vendor blogs, and independent practitioner posts), and because the TUI-framework-regression pattern (Topic 5), while convergent, rests on likely/assumed evidence rather than a single confirmed comparative study.

## Open Questions

- IF the CHI '21 paper's full text (currently inaccessible, 403 both attempts) contains a formal taxonomy or severity ranking of CLI accessibility failures THEN the six-topic organization above should be revised to match that taxonomy rather than this synthesis's inferred grouping, and rules currently marked "likely" via secondary paraphrase (1.2 CHI-paraphrase items, 4.1 detail beyond the abstract) should be re-confidence-rated against the primary source.
- IF Textual, Ratatui, or Bubble Tea ship confirmed, tested screen-reader support after this research's cutoff THEN the Topic 5 recommendation (avoid full-screen TUI frameworks by default) should be narrowed to name only the frameworks still lacking support, rather than applying blanket caution to the category.
- IF the Claude Code Issue #247 claim (box-drawing characters read verbosely) is confirmed from the primary issue text rather than a search summary THEN it should be promoted from likely to confirmed and can be cited standalone rather than only in aggregate with the ANSI-escape-code pattern.
- IF a target user population is predominantly using GTK-based terminal emulators (gnome-terminal, xfce4-terminal, mate-terminal) rather than XTerm/urxvt/st/Konsole THEN the terminal-emulator-choice finding (5.8) becomes a non-issue for that population and the spec's scope can drop terminal-emulator compatibility as a requirement — but this should be verified against actual user telemetry, not assumed.
- IF the xogium.me "text mode lie" article's core claim (VT100 scrolling-region-based CLIs are more accessible than canvas-redrawing TUIs) is independently confirmed by a second source THEN the Topic 5 recommendation should be strengthened from "treat as risk-bearing, require fallback" to "avoid outright, prefer scrolling-region-based rendering by default."

There is no standardized "accessibility tree" analogous to the DOM/ARIA — a terminal is structurally an unstructured text stream (CHI '21 paper, confirmed). ## Six Topic Areas, With Checkable Rules

**1. Output streams, machine-readability, exit codes** — stdout for primary output, stderr for diagnostics (clig.dev, confirmed); zero/non-zero exit codes (confirmed); `--json`/`--plain` machine-readable modes (confirmed) — these double as the workaround screen-reader users actually rely on (CHI paper). Key gap: TTY-detection alone can't distinguish "human with screen reader" from "human at plain terminal," so accessibility can't hook into TTY checks alone — it needs explicit flags.

**2. **3. Animation/spinners** — the strongest, most repeated confirmed failure pattern. Animated spinners are "extremely problematic for screen readers" (Seirdy); GitHub CLI's braille-character spinner literally confused screen readers and was replaced with static text (GitHub blog, confirmed); Anthropic's own Claude Code has an open issue (#11002) where NVDA freezes during token-streaming/spinner updates, described as "largely unusable" for accessibility-focused Windows users; even GitHub Copilot CLI's shipped `--screen-reader` mode has a live regression re-announcing a status value on every keypress (cli/copilot-cli#1642) — evidence that shipping a flag isn't sufficient without interaction testing.

**4. Structural semantics** — CLIs lack any accessibility-tree equivalent to HTML/DOM (CHI paper, root cause of most other findings); provide text alternatives for ASCII art, opt-in only via flags (AFixt); box-drawing characters get announced verbosely ("box drawing light horizontal") per Claude Code issue #247 (likely, secondary-source only); unstripped ANSI escape codes get read aloud as literal garbage (likely); man pages' standardized, searchable format is a positive pattern worth preserving (Seirdy).

## Honest Gap Assessment

- The one peer-reviewed source (CHI '21, Sampath/Merrick/Macvean, ACM DL) had its full text blocked by a 403 on both fetch attempts — findings from it beyond the abstract are secondary paraphrases, not confirmed direct reads.
- No sustained conference-talk circuit specific to CLI/terminal accessibility was found for 2023–2026; the field runs on one paper, scattered blog posts of uneven rigor, and vendor postmortems rather than proactive research.
- clig.dev, despite being the most-cited CLI guidelines document, has no dedicated accessibility section — its relevance is incidental.

## Recommendation (medium confidence)

Default new CLI/TUI work to plain/static/structured output (topics 1–4, high-confidence, multiply-corroborated); treat any full-screen TUI framework as accessibility-risk-bearing by default and require a static/linear fallback before shipping (topic 5, weaker per-source but strong in aggregate across four independent frameworks); require real screen-reader or espeak-ng testing as a release gate, since every confirmed production failure found (GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code) was interactive/behavioral and passed normal code review undetected.</result>

content.text:
# Accessibility in the Wisp Pipeline — Report & Proposal

## Where a11y actually belongs in the workflow

Every research thread converges on the same answer: **accessibility has to enter at spec time, not audit time.** Microsoft's 2025/2026 eval found baseline LLM code passes only ~12% of accessibility checks, jumping to ~60% when given explicit, structured a11y criteria *before generation* — the single largest lever isn't better scanning, it's better requirements. BBC's design-review process and Deque's a11yAC methodology both write accessibility into the artifact that crosses the design→build boundary, not into a later checklist. So: **primary integration point is Design (Scribe + Muse)**, with a real but secondary integration point at **Verify (Ranger)** for the machine-checkable subset, and light-touch integration at **Define (Weaver)** and **Build (Navigator/Smith)** that mostly falls out of capability we already have.

No new schema is needed anywhere in this proposal — verified `spec@1.acceptance_criteria` and `candidate@1.taxonomy` are both free-text/unconstrained, so everything below slots into existing shapes.

## What the research actually says

**WCAG, condensed for this pipeline's purposes:** 86 success criteria across POUR (Perceivable/Operable/Understandable/Robust) × A/AA/AAA. Roughly 30–40% are genuinely machine-checkable (missing alt text, missing labels, contrast ratio, heading order, ARIA name/role/value, `lang` attribute); the rest require human or specialist judgment (whether alt text is *meaningfully* descriptive, whether a flow is *understandable*). Deque's own axe-core states plainly: **no AA criterion can be fully satisfied by automation alone.** That's a boundary this proposal respects rather than papers over — Ranger will be told explicitly what it can confirm versus what it must flag for a human.

**The best template for testable a11y criteria** is Deque's **a11yAC**: accessibility acceptance criteria written Given-When-Then, in the same story as functional criteria, naming *assistive-tech-observable semantics* rather than visual description:

> Given I am a blind screen reader user, and I have submitted the form, and a loading spinner is visible, When I navigate to the spinner, Then I hear the role, and I hear the text "loading."

This is essentially the same discipline our `spec@1` acceptance criteria already require (falsifiable, no implementation assumptions) — a11yAC just names the specific shape that discipline should take for accessibility.

**BBC's practice** adds one artifact type worth borrowing: an explicit **screen-reader experience narrative** written at design time for any genuinely novel interactive pattern — not needed for a plain button, valuable for a custom widget.

**CLI accessibility has no WCAG equivalent** — no ratified standard exists. What's real and multiply-corroborated: stdout/stderr separation, exit code discipline, `--json`/`--plain` modes, honoring `NO_COLOR`, never encoding meaning in color alone, and — the single strongest finding — **animation/spinners are the most common real-world failure**. GitHub CLI's spinner confused screen readers and was replaced with static text. Worth flagging directly: **Claude Code itself has an open issue (#11002) where NVDA freezes during token-streaming/spinner updates.** The counter-intuitive finding: a plain scrollback CLI with a static-text mode is currently *more* accessible than a modern full-screen TUI, because terminals have no accessibility-tree equivalent to the DOM — full-screen redraws break screen readers that plain scrollback doesn't.

## Current state (verified directly, not assumed)

- **Muse** already has real depth: role/name/focus-order/keyboard/live-region criteria are required in every component spec, and its auditor already rejects "looks disabled" in favor of "carries `aria-disabled`, leaves tab order, emits no `onClick`." This is close to a11yAC quality already — it just needs the Given-When-Then framing made explicit and the BBC-style narrative added for novel patterns.
- **Scribe has zero a11y awareness.** This is the real gap, because not everything user-facing is "a UI component" — a CLI tool spec, or a general feature spec with user-facing output, goes through Scribe, not Muse. Right now those specs get no accessibility prompting at all.
- **Ranger has zero code-level a11y scanning** — no hazard taxonomy file exists for it.
- **No CLI accessibility consideration exists anywhere in the repo.**

## The proposal

**1. Scribe (`drafter.md`) — close the general-spec gap.**
Add conditional judgment: when a spec involves user-facing interaction (UI *or* CLI) and the artifact isn't routed to Muse, the drafter includes accessibility acceptance criteria in Deque's Given-When-Then shape — naming role/state/announcement for UI, or stream/exit-code/color/mode behavior for CLI. This is the single highest-leverage change: it's the difference between 12% and 60% in the Microsoft study, applied to the plugin that currently has no a11y path at all.

**2. Scribe (`auditor.md`) — reject vague criteria.**
Extend the same discipline Muse's auditor already has: an accessibility criterion that says "must be accessible" or "should work with screen readers" is rejected as a spec smell, citing WCAG's own formal testability bar (objectively answerable, or reaching high inter-rater agreement) as the objective standard. One paragraph addition.

**3. Muse (`drafter.md`) — formalize the criterion shape, add the narrative artifact.**
Reframe existing accessibility criteria explicitly as Given-When-Then a11yAC (mostly a phrasing tightening, not new capability — Muse is already close). Add a new criterion category, gated to genuinely novel interactive patterns only (not every button): an explicit assistive-tech experience narrative, modeled on BBC's design-review deliverable.

**4. New reference file: `shared/references/a11y-hazards.md`, loaded by Ranger.**
Modeled directly on axe-core's rule shape (the first research thread's concrete recommendation): each entry gets an id, severity/impact, WCAG SC reference, description, and a grep-able or read-able detection heuristic — scoped honestly to what a source-reading scanner can actually confirm: missing `alt`, missing accessible name on custom interactive elements, click handlers with no keyboard equivalent or role, positive `tabindex`, color-only status text, missing `lang`. **Explicitly excludes contrast-ratio checking** — that needs computed/rendered styles, not source reading, and claiming Ranger can do it would be exactly the false-confidence the research warns against. New taxonomy prefix `A` (A1–A6), fitting Ranger's existing T1–T10 convention with no schema change.

**5. New reference file: `shared/references/cli-a11y-hazards.md`, loaded by Ranger when recon detects a CLI surface** (bin field in package.json, `[[bin]]` in Cargo.toml, or a CLI-parsing dependency). Entries: missing `NO_COLOR`/`isTTY` branching before ANSI color output, animation/spinner with no static-text fallback (the single most-confirmed real failure mode found), missing `--json`/`--plain` output mode, interactive-only prompts with no non-interactive path, non-standard exit codes. All genuinely detectable via source reading — no rendering required.

**6. Ranger (`scanner.md`, `adversary.md`) — wire both files into the default scan**, same routing pattern already used for the T7/T10 split; no new agent needed, no boundary-tracer needed (these hazards don't need field-survival tracing, they need the same read-and-judge shape as T1–T9).

**7. Smith (`implementer.md`) — one judgment addition, not a new agent.**
When a task covers an accessibility criterion, the failing test should be an actual automated assertion where the criterion is machine-checkable (axe-core/jest-axe for web, structured-output/exit-code assertions for CLI); when the criterion is judgment-only (per WCAG's own boundary), the test still exists but is flagged for human/specialist review rather than silently claiming automated coverage — this is CodeA11y's "Reminder agent" pattern, folded into Smith's existing judgment rather than a new agent.

**8. Navigator, Sentinel — no changes needed.**
Navigator's `challenger` already rejects orphaned criteria with no covering task — a11y criteria get that protection for free once Scribe/Muse actually produce them. Sentinel already gates any artifact against its criteria — nothing a11y-specific to add.

**9. The repair loop already exists — just needs a11y findings to feed it.**
A11YRepair's "generate → scan → gate on strictly-decreasing violations → rollback and reprompt" pattern is architecturally identical to this repo's existing blockers-only retry loop (constitution's Axiom Retry Caller Constraint, now Sentinel). No new mechanism — Ranger just needs the taxonomy to have something to feed into it.

## What I'd explicitly *not* do

- No new schema — confirmed both `spec@1` and `candidate@1` already accommodate everything above.
- No new plugin, no new agent — everything above is a reference file plus targeted judgment additions to agents that already exist.
- No claim that Ranger can check contrast, meaningful alt-text quality, or workflow understandability — the research is unanimous that these need a human or a real rendering tool, and I'd rather the taxonomy be honest about that boundary than produce false confidence.

## Build order

1. `shared/references/a11y-hazards.md` + `cli-a11y-hazards.md` (self-contained, no dependencies)
2. Wire both into Ranger's scanner/adversary
3. Scribe drafter + auditor additions (unblocks the highest-leverage gap)
4. Muse drafter's Given-When-Then reframe + narrative criterion (smaller, since Muse is already close)
5. Smith implementer's machine-checkable-vs-judgment test guidance

Want me to start implementing, beginning with the two reference files since everything else depends on the taxonomy existing?

message.content: How does a11yAC change any of our perspective on the rest of our workflows too?

content.text:
Three things generalize beyond accessibility, and they're worth pulling into the constitution's own criterion-writing guidance, not just Scribe/Muse's a11y-specific additions:

**1. Given-When-Then's explicit "Given" clause is missing from our current criterion style, and it's probably a real gap.** Our criteria today are mostly single declarative sentences ("when `disabled` is true, X") — the context is often implicit. A lot of what makes a criterion ambiguous isn't the assertion, it's an unstated precondition. Making "Given" mandatory in the constitution's own definition of a testable criterion — not just for a11y — would likely catch a class of vague criteria our auditors currently only catch indirectly.

**2. WCAG's formal definition of "testable" is sharper than ours and should probably replace it.** Right now the constitution/drafters define testable as "confirmable by a tester with no implementation knowledge." WCAG's bar is more precise: *objectively answerable by automation, or reaching high inter-rater agreement among independent evaluators.* That second clause is doing real work — it's what licenses a criterion like "the error message clearly explains the fix" to count as testable (multiple evaluators would agree) without collapsing into "must be accessible"-style vagueness. This maps directly onto the `judgment_call` flag that already exists in our schemas — it's currently under-specified what makes something a legitimate judgment call versus a smell, and WCAG's inter-rater-agreement framing is a genuinely better answer than what we have now, applicable to every plugin that drafts criteria, not just Muse.

**3. "Bad to better" validates an escape valve we already built but don't invoke deliberately.** WCAG's own "there is no 100% accessible" and Pickering's rejection of pass/fail perfectionism initially look like a challenge to Sentinel/Scribe's binary, default-fail exit-gate discipline — but we already have the right pressure valve for this: the constitution's Epistemic Stopping rule demotes disputed items to non-blocking `api_notes` after round 2 rather than looping forever. The a11y research suggests that escape valve should be *named* as the deliberate landing spot for judgment-only criteria (an a11y criterion needing human/specialist confirmation, but also any other subjective-quality criterion) rather than something that only kicks in accidentally when two adversarial rounds run out. Not new architecture — just a clearer contract for when to reach for it.

None of these require new schemas or agents — they're constitution-level refinements to how *any* criterion gets written and judged, that accessibility happened to force into the open. Want me to fold these three into `shared/constitution.md` and the relevant drafter/auditor agents as part of the same pass, or keep them separate from the a11y build itself?

message.content: Should it just be constitution level or should we consider BDD more holistically too? How does it work with SDD and TDD? DOes it conflict? How do we account for in the spec of SDD and the testing of TDD?

content.text:
Worth thinking through properly rather than just bolting Given-When-Then onto the constitution, because the answer changes what I'd actually touch.

**The three aren't competing paradigms — they answer different questions, and BDD sits *between* the other two.** SDD (Scribe/Muse) answers "what's the durable, drift-detectable contract." TDD (Smith) answers "in what order do code and test get written, and how do we prove the test would actually catch a regression." BDD, properly understood (Dan North coined it explicitly as a *refinement* of TDD, not an alternative to it), answers a narrower question: "what *shape* should a behavior scenario take so it's unambiguous and translates cleanly into a test." Given-When-Then scenarios are, in classic BDD tooling, often executed *directly* as the test (Cucumber compiles a Gherkin scenario straight into a test run). So the honest mapping onto our architecture: BDD doesn't sit alongside SDD and TDD, it sits **in the seam between them** — it's a phrasing discipline for the artifact that Scribe produces and Smith consumes.

**Where it doesn't conflict:** BDD's "three amigos" principle (no single person holds enough context to write good scenarios alone) is the same argument that already justifies our drafter/auditor/verifier split — we're already doing BDD's distributed-judgment idea, just with agents instead of a meeting. No architectural tension there, just a naming confirmation.

**Where it would conflict, if adopted the wrong way:** Classic BDD is usually bound to specific tooling — Cucumber, SpecFlow, Gherkin `.feature` files, step-definition glue code. That tooling requirement is a real conflict: Smith's implementer currently reads whatever test framework a target codebase already uses (Jest, pytest, cargo test) and writes idiomatic tests in it. Mandating Gherkin/Cucumber across every consuming project would be exactly the kind of invasive, framework-opinionated imposition this ecosystem deliberately avoids. So the answer isn't "adopt BDD holistically" in the sense of adopting its tooling — it's "adopt BDD's scenario-writing discipline without its tooling requirement." Given-When-Then as prose structure in `acceptance_criteria`, not Given-When-Then as an executable `.feature` file.

**Concretely, this changes where I'd touch things — one more surface than I said last turn:**

- **Constitution**: the Given-When-Then phrasing rule and the WCAG-derived testability bar, as discussed — ecosystem-wide, affects both Scribe and Muse.
- **Navigator's `planner.md`** — this is the piece I'd missed. Once a criterion is Given-When-Then shaped, the planner's job of "write the exact failing test" stops being a loose translation from prose intent to test code and becomes close to mechanical: Given → test setup/fixtures, When → the action under test, Then → the assertion. Worth a small judgment note there specifically, since that's the actual seam where spec-language and test-code currently have the most room to drift apart from each other without anyone noticing — tightening that translation fidelity is the real payoff of doing this, more than the constitution wording itself.
- **Smith** — no change beyond what's already proposed. If the planner hands it a Given/When/Then-faithful test skeleton, Smith's TDD cycle doesn't need to know BDD exists at all.
- **Not Weaver** — Given-When-Then is a shape for *acceptance criteria* specifically, not raw need statements. Formalizing that early would over-constrain before enough is known, which is also how BDD itself treats it (scenarios get written once a feature is being specified, not at the raw idea stage).

So: constitution-level for the rule itself, plus one targeted addition to Navigator's planner for the seam where it actually pays off. Want me to implement both together?

input.description: Research Martin Fowler on BDD/TDD/SDD
input.prompt:
Research Martin Fowler's (and ThoughtWorks') published thinking on how Behavior-Driven Development, Test-Driven Development, and Specification/Spec-Driven Development relate to each other. Search the web for real sources — don't rely on memory alone, his bliki (martinfowler.com/bliki) has many short, specific entries worth finding directly.

Cover:
1. Fowler's own writing on BDD — how he characterizes its relationship to TDD (he's written that BDD emerged partly to fix confusion/misuse of TDD, e.g. around what to test and how to name tests). Find his actual articles/bliki entries on this (search "martinfowler.com bliki BDD", "martinfowler.com GivenWhenThen").
2. Fowler's writing on "Specification by Example" (the book by Gojko Adzic, which Fowler wrote the foreword for or endorsed) and "Living Documentation" — the idea that executable specifications double as both requirements and tests. Find what Fowler specifically says is the value and the risks/failure modes of this approach.
3. Dan North's original 2006 BDD writings (northconcepts / dannorth.net) since Fowler frequently references North as BDD's originator — find North's own framing of "BDD is TDD done right" or similar, and what specific problem BDD was solving that plain TDD wasn't.
4. Any recent (2024-2026) writing from Fowler, ThoughtWorks, or the ThoughtWorks Technology Radar specifically about AI-assisted/agentic software development practices, spec-driven development for AI coding agents, or how BDD/TDD change (or don't) when an LLM agent is doing the implementation instead of a human. Search "ThoughtWorks technology radar AI agents 2026", "Martin Fowler AI coding agents", "ThoughtWorks spec-driven AI development".
5. Any writing on the failure modes / criticisms of BDD in practice (e.g. "Gherkin scenarios become stale," "BDD tooling overhead," teams writing Given-When-Then without the collaborative discovery process that makes it valuable) — this matters because we want the substance without the tooling overhead.

Return a structured findings report with direct quotes/paraphrases and sources cited. Be honest about what you couldn't find (e.g. if there's little-to-no recent Fowler/ThoughtWorks commentary specifically on AI agentic dev + BDD/TDD, say so plainly rather than stretching older material to fit).

input.description: Research Kent C. Dodds testing philosophy and NN/g crossover
input.prompt:
Research Kent C. Dodds' published testing philosophy, and separately check for any Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g) material relevant to structured specs / behavior-driven thinking / AI-agent workflows. Search the web for real sources.

Part 1 — Kent C. Dodds (kentcdodds.com, his blog, testingjavascript.com material, conference talks):
1. His "Testing Trophy" concept — how it reframes the classic testing pyramid, and how it relates to (or reacts against) strict TDD unit-test-heavy practices. Find his actual writing (search "kentcdodds.com testing trophy", "write tests not too many mostly integration").
2. His stated philosophy on what makes a good test — he's written specifically about testing implementation details vs. testing behavior/user-facing outcomes (this is directly relevant to BDD's "test behavior not implementation" principle) — find his actual framing and whether he explicitly connects it to BDD language or not.
3. Any recent (2024-2026) commentary from Dodds specifically on AI coding agents, AI-assisted testing, or how test-writing practices should change (or shouldn't) when an LLM is generating code — search "Kent C Dodds AI agents testing", "Kent C Dodds 2026". input.description: Research agentic SDD/BDD/TDD industry leaders and companies
input.prompt:
Research how companies and industry leaders building AI coding agent tools and methodologies are actually combining Spec-Driven Development, Behavior-Driven Development, and Test-Driven Development for AI-agent-written code, as of 2025-2026. This is the most directly relevant research thread — search the web thoroughly, this is a fast-moving space with real recent material.

Specifically investigate:
1. **Amazon's "Kiro"** — an AI IDE explicitly built around spec-driven development for AI agents. Find their actual documentation/blog posts on how their spec-driven workflow works, what an "spec" looks like in Kiro, and whether/how they incorporate behavior-scenario or test-driven elements.
2. **GitHub's "Spec Kit"** (githubnext or similar) or any GitHub-published guidance on spec-driven AI development workflows — search "GitHub Spec Kit", "GitHub spec-driven development AI agents".
3. **Tessl** — a company founded by Guy Podjarny (former Snyk CEO) explicitly built around "spec-driven development" as a category for AI-native software. Find their public writing/manifesto on what spec-driven development means for them, and how it relates to testing.
4. Other AI coding agent products' published methodology: Cursor's "plan mode"/rules files, Windsurf/Cascade, Replit Agent, Cognition Labs' Devin, Amp, or any other AI coding agent that has published specific guidance on how they structure specs/plans/tests for agent-driven implementation. Search broadly for "AI coding agent spec driven development 2026", "agentic TDD", "agentic BDD".
5. Any published synthesis or industry commentary (blog posts, conference talks, InfoQ/ThoughtWorks-adjacent sources) specifically arguing for or against combining BDD+SDD+TDD in an agentic pipeline — i.e., does anyone explicitly argue these three practices compose well together for AI agents, or that one subsumes the others when an LLM is doing the work?
6. Any critical/skeptical takes — search for pushback on "spec-driven development" as a buzzword, concerns about AI agents producing verbose but low-quality specs, or evidence that BDD-style scenarios written by/for AI agents don't deliver the same collaborative-discovery value they do for human teams.

Return a structured findings report covering each company/practice found, with direct sourcing. This is meant to inform whether a specific AI coding agent plugin ecosystem (which already does spec-drafting -> planning -> TDD implementation -> verification gates) should adopt BDD-style Given-When-Then phrasing in its specs. Flag anything found that's a direct precedent or counter-argument for that specific decision.

- Dodds explicitly frames this as a reaction to Martin Fowler's classic Testing Pyramid, arguing the pyramid's core assumption — that lower-level tests should dominate because higher-level tests are slow/expensive/brittle — no longer holds: "our tools are awesome now and this assumption is less true."
- The Trophy shape, bottom to top: **static analysis** (linting/TypeScript) as the base, then a wide band of **integration tests** (the largest recommended investment), a smaller band of **unit tests**, and a thin cap of **end-to-end tests**.
- This is a direct reaction against strict, unit-test-heavy TDD orthodoxy. He argues unit tests in isolation "doesn't do you any good if you don't also verify that they work together properly," and that chasing 100% unit coverage produces diminishing returns and pushes people toward testing implementation details rather than real behavior. - Net effect: integration tests (not unit tests) are positioned as the best confidence-to-cost tradeoff — the tagline being "write tests, not too many, mostly integration."

**2. Implementation Details vs. Behavior**

Source: [Testing Implementation Details](https://kentcdodds.com/blog/testing-implementation-details)

- Core quote: "The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you."

<result>I have enough material now to compile a thorough, well-cited report. Let me deliver the findings.

# Findings Report: Fowler/ThoughtWorks on BDD, TDD, and Spec-Driven Development

## 1. Fowler's own writing on BDD's relationship to TDD

Fowler does **not** have a dedicated bliki entry titled "Behavior-Driven Development" — I confirmed this by direct search; his closest and most-cited entry is **[Given-When-Then](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/GivenWhenThen.html)**. In it, Fowler:
- Credits **Daniel Terhorst-North and Chris Matts** as developers of the Given-When-Then style within BDD, noting North himself credits Ivan Moore for "a significant amount of inspiration."
- Frames Given-When-Then as "a reformulation of the Four-Phase Test pattern" (Meszaros: Setup/Exercise/Verify/Teardown) and notes the equivalent "Arrange, Act, Assert" (Bill Wake) — i.e., Fowler treats BDD's structuring convention as a **parallel naming style**, not a superior method: "Test frameworks tend to follow either naming style of xunit or BDD."
- Notably, this entry does **not** explicitly argue BDD fixes TDD's problems — that argument lives more with Dan North than with Fowler directly.

Fowler's **[Unit Test](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/UnitTest.html)** bliki entry is relevant background: he calls unit-testing terminology "ill-defined" and suggests "xunit testing" might be a clearer term than "unit testing," tracing the lineage Extreme Programming → xunit-style testing → TDD → (BDD as a naming/vocabulary correction downstream).

His **[Specification By Example](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/SpecificationByExample.html)** entry (he says he coined the term in 2002) is his fullest treatment of the underlying idea BDD formalizes:
- Pushes back on treating tests as a mere "side effect" of TDD, using the analogy: "if someone offered me a million dollars to hike up a mountain... the side-effect to my wallet is hardly trivial."
- States the "double-check principle": good TDD practice means you "always say things twice: once in the code and once in the tests" — redundancy via different expression methods catches errors.
- States explicit limitations: "Specification By Example isn't enough... you need to do more to ensure everything is properly communicated," and "tests are always going to be incomplete." He also flags the classic gaming risk: a supplier could "just return hard-coded responses to the specific test inputs" rather than a general solution.
- Requires collaborative context to work: needs "both sides... collaborating and not fighting," plus supplementary practices (conversation, DDD, contractual thinking).

**Caveat:** I could not find a Fowler-authored piece that explicitly narrates "BDD emerged to fix TDD misuse" in his own voice with that framing — that specific narrative is Dan North's own account (see #3), which Fowler references/links to but doesn't restate as his own argument. Treat any claim that Fowler personally wrote "BDD fixes TDD's confusion" as **unsupported by what I found** — the framing belongs to North; Fowler's contribution is more the Given-When-Then/Specification-by-Example vocabulary layer.

## 2. Specification by Example / Living Documentation

- Fowler is credited with coining "Specification by Example" in 2002 (per multiple secondary sources, e.g. Gojko Adzic's own retrospective at [gojko.net/2020/03/17/sbe-10-years.html](https://gojko.net/2020/03/17/sbe-10-years.html)).
- I could **not confirm** that Fowler wrote a foreword to Adzic's 2011 book *Specification by Example: How Successful Teams Deliver the Right Software*. Search results consistently link Fowler to the *term's* origin but never surface foreword/endorsement text. **I'm not able to verify this claim from the sources found — treat it as unconfirmed, possibly conflating "coined the term" with "endorsed the book."**
- The value/risk framing Fowler gives (his own bliki, not the book) is captured above: value = tests double as specification and catch a class of errors formal specs miss cheaply; risk = incompleteness, the "hard-coded response" gaming risk, and the requirement of genuine collaboration or the technique degrades.

## 3. Dan North's original BDD framing (2006)

From **["Introducing BDD"](https://dannorth.net/blog/introducing-bdd/)** (Better Software magazine, March 2006):
- The problem BDD solved: "Programmers wanted to know where to start, what to test and what not to test, how much to test in one go, what to call their tests, and how to understand why a test fails." North felt TDD, as commonly taught, "presented itself as a series of pitfalls" rather than a clear path.
- The fix was largely **linguistic**: replacing "test" with "behaviour" dissolved a category of confusion, because it reoriented developers from "what to test" (an open-ended, anxiety-inducing question) to "what should the system do" (a scoped, natural-language question).
- Concrete naming convention: "Test method names should be sentences," using a "should" template ("the class should do X") to keep each test single-responsibility.
- North extended this past unit-test naming into requirements/analysis — proposing a shared "ubiquitous language" so business stakeholders, analysts, testers, and developers describe behavior in the same vocabulary (this is the direct ancestor of Given-When-Then and Gherkin).
- Background: North started replacing JUnit with **JBehave** at the end of 2003, specifically to strip "testing" vocabulary and rebuild around "verifying behaviour."

So the "BDD is TDD done right" framing is substantiated, but as **North's own claim about his own motivation**, not literally that exact phrase turning up verbatim in what I fetched — it's a fair paraphrase of "TDD but with the confusions removed," which is what North states directly.

## 4. Recent (2024–2026) Fowler/ThoughtWorks writing on AI-assisted development

This is the richest vein, and directly relevant to your use case:

**Martin Fowler's "Exploring Gen AI" series** (martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/) is an ongoing set of memos from Fowler and Thoughtworks colleagues, spanning 2023–2025+.

- **["TDD inside the agent loop – theater or actual value?"](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/tdd-in-the-agent-loop.html)** by **Birgitta Böckeler** is the single most on-point source found. Key claims:
  - Empirically (Opus-judged quality comparisons), "there was no clearly discernible difference based on TDD workflow versus no TDD workflow" — non-TDD runs sometimes scored *higher* on design and test quality.
  - Diagnosis of why: "The way AI agents were trained is that they have seen completed functions and descriptions of those functions. The number of actual step-by-step TDD examples they have seen is a tiny part of the training data" — i.e., the step-by-step red/green/refactor *process* isn't well-represented in training data the way finished code is.
  - TDD's classic benefits don't clearly transfer to agents: test-tautology avoidance was unresolved (agents wrote self-referential tests anyway), the "small steps for feedback" benefit is questionable when an agent debugs fine without incrementalism, and the confidence-building/psychological benefit of TDD (for a human) doesn't apply to a non-human implementer.
  - Costs: TDD approaches used 3–8x more tokens; prescriptive TDD prompting requires continuous re-tuning across model versions.
  - Mutation-testing comparison showed **no regression-quality advantage** for TDD vs non-TDD runs.
  - Her conclusion: she has "abandoned prescriptive TDD instructions" in favor of mutation testing, static/modularity analysis, an "Approved Scenarios" pattern, and automated refactor triggers. Verbatim: "Whatever ends up giving us trust and confidence in our software in the future — I think the role of TDD as we've known it is significantly smaller than pre-GenAI."

- **["Understanding Spec-Driven Development: Kiro, spec-kit, and Tessl"](https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/sdd-3-tools.html)**, also by Böckeler, gives a taxonomy that's become the field's working vocabulary:
  - **Spec-first**: spec written up front, used to generate code once, then discarded/not maintained.
  - **Spec-anchored**: spec persists alongside code as the durable source of intent; when requirements change, the spec updates first; agents reading the codebase later are pointed at the spec, not just the code.
  - **Spec-as-source**: "the spec is the main source file over time, and only the spec is edited by the human, the human never touches the code" — code is generated and marked `// GENERATED FROM SPEC — DO NOT EDIT`.
  - She notes Kiro's acceptance-criteria format explicitly reuses **Given-When-Then** — a direct, current lineage line from Dan North's 2006 BDD vocabulary into 2025 AI-agent spec tooling.
  - Stated risks: agents frequently **ignore** detailed specs/notes ("the agent ignored the notes... it just took them as a new specification and generated them all over again, creating duplicates"); a "false control illusion" from elaborate spec workflows that agents don't reliably follow; explicit parallel drawn to historical **Model-Driven Development** failures (inflexibility, overhead); and observed **non-determinism** even at low abstraction — regenerating from the same spec produces different code.

- **ThoughtWorks Technology Radar** (Volume 34, ~April 2026) has a dedicated **["Spec-driven development" entry](https://www.thoughtworks.com/en-us/radar/techniques/spec-driven-development)**:
  - Frames SDD as "workflows beginning with a structured functional specification, then proceeding through multiple steps to break it down into smaller pieces, solutions and tasks," generally following spec → plan → implement.
  - Names OpenSpec, GitHub Spec Kit, and Amazon Kiro as tools standardizing the practice.
  - Frames spec-driven development and Agent Skills as "feedforward controls" and mutation testing as a "feedback control" that triggers self-correction before human review — i.e., ThoughtWorks is explicitly positioning spec-driven practice and mutation testing (not classic TDD) as the emerging AI-era control mechanisms.
  - The overall Radar release (per Morningstar/ThoughtWorks press coverage) is themed around "a return to engineering fundamentals to combat cognitive debt" as AI accelerates complexity — worth reading if you want the broader framing, but I did not fetch that full press piece for direct quotes.
  - Also names the "Ralph Loop" pattern (single agent, infinite loop, fresh context per iteration, implementing one spec-piece at a time) as a related emerging pattern.

## Research Findings: SDD + BDD + TDD Convergence for AI Coding Agents (2025–2026)

### 1. Amazon Kiro — spec-driven, EARS not Gherkin
Kiro (launched July 2025, AWS) runs a three-phase pipeline: requirements → design → tasks, with explicit traceability between phases. Its "Specs" feature converts requirements into **EARS notation** (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) — `WHEN [event] THEN [system] SHALL [response]`, plus `IF`/`WHILE`/`WHERE` variants — not Given-When-Then/Gherkin. EARS criteria are deliberately "unambiguous and testable... easy to translate into test cases." Kiro's hook system separately triggers test-file updates on save/change, but this is automation glue, not a BDD layer. **Direct precedent for structured, machine-parseable acceptance-criteria syntax, but Kiro's own choice was EARS over Given-When-Then** — worth noting since your plugin already resembles the EARS style per your own CLAUDE.md ("EARS-format authoritative rules").
Sources: [kiro.dev/blog/introducing-kiro](https://kiro.dev/blog/introducing-kiro/), [kiro.dev/docs/specs/feature-specs/requirements-first](https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/feature-specs/requirements-first/), [Forbes on Kiro launch](https://www.forbes.com/sites/janakirammsv/2025/07/15/aws-launches-kiro-a-specification-driven-agentic-ide/)

### 2. GitHub Spec Kit — explicit BDD adoption
GitHub's open-source Spec Kit (Sept 2025) pipeline is spec → plan → tasks → implementation, working with 30+ coding agents. Its spec template **explicitly uses Given/When/Then**: "Acceptance Scenarios" per user story are written in that format, each story independently testable and prioritized (P1/P2/P3), plus tagged functional requirements (FR-NNN) and measurable success criteria (SC-NNN). A community extension (spec-kit-reqnroll-bdd) goes further, converting acceptance criteria directly into Gherkin `.feature` files with `@AC-001`-style tags for full BDD tooling integration. **This is the strongest direct precedent for your question** — a major, widely-adopted spec-driven AI tool chose Given-When-Then as its acceptance-scenario format, not EARS-style SHALL statements.
Sources: [github.com/github/spec-kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit), [spec-kit/templates/spec-template.md](https://github.com/github/spec-kit/blob/main/templates/spec-template.md), [github.blog spec-driven-development](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/generative-ai/spec-driven-development-with-ai-get-started-with-a-new-open-source-toolkit/)

### 3. Tessl (Guy Podjarny) — specs "bolstered by tests," not BDD-branded
Tessl's framing: agents "hallucinate APIs, claim success when they've failed, and jump straight into coding without clarifying intent." Their fix is specs as the durable artifact, "bolstered by tests and hard guardrails," with the Tessl Framework pairing specs with auto-generated aligned tests to enforce guardrails as the app evolves, plus a Spec Registry (10,000+ specs) preventing library-API hallucination. Podjarny predicts most 2026 development will be "at least spec-assisted." **Tessl does not use Given-When-Then language publicly** — their vocabulary is spec+test pairing, not scenario-based BDD. Testing is positioned as an enforcement mechanism for specs, not a discovery/collaboration practice.
Sources: [tessl.io/blog/tessl-launches-spec-driven-framework-and-registry](https://tessl.io/blog/tessl-launches-spec-driven-framework-and-registry), [zuplo.com/blog/spec-driven-ai-development](https://zuplo.com/blog/spec-driven-ai-development), [tessl.io/blog/how-tessls-products-pioneer-spec-driven-development](https://tessl.io/blog/how-tessls-products-pioneer-spec-driven-development)

### 4. Other agent products
- **Cursor**: "Plan Mode" enforces Research → Clarify → Plan → Build, explicitly separating planning from coding ("AI coding usually fails when models plan and code at the same time"). No published BDD/Gherkin convention — plans are freeform, refined through iterative questioning until "no room for misinterpretation."
- **Cognition/Devin**: Plan → code → test → ship loop with repo-specific "Playbooks" for conventions; no published spec syntax or BDD adoption found.
- No public methodology found for Windsurf/Cascade, Replit Agent, or Amp specifically addressing BDD/TDD/SDD combination beyond generic "plan then execute" patterns.
Sources: [cursor.com/blog/agent-best-practices](https://cursor.com/blog/agent-best-practices), [cognition.com/blog/introducing-devin](https://cognition.com/blog/introducing-devin)

### 5. Explicit synthesis arguments (BDD+SDD+TDD composing)
- **ThoughtWorks** (Nov 2025, placed SDD in Radar "Assess" ring): explicitly states "**TDD is SDD at the unit level**, and SDD extends this thinking to higher levels." "**BDD is the most direct ancestor of modern SDD**, with Gherkin scenarios as executable specifications." Recommends borrowing BDD's Given/When/Then and "domain-oriented ubiquitous language" for spec-writing, while TDD still drives interface design at the unit level — i.e., **three practices at three altitudes, not competing**. Caveats: no systematic way to eval specs yet; spec drift/hallucination hard to avoid; over-formalized specs risk "waterfall's pitfalls."
- **Sean Grove's "The New Code" (OpenAI, AI Engineer World's Fair 2025)** — the founding talk cited as SDD's origin story: code is only 10-20% of a programmer's value, specs are the real source-of-truth artifact ("shredding the source and carefully version-controlling the binary" describes prompt-then-discard workflows). Doesn't address BDD/TDD directly but is the philosophical root everyone else cites.
- **TDAD (Test-Driven Agentic Development, arXiv 2603.17973)**: an explicit synthesis paper — behavioral specs compiled into executable test suites by one agent, a second agent iterates implementation against them, mutation testing validates the tests. Reduced regressions 70% (6.08%→1.82%) vs vanilla baseline. This is very close to your ecosystem's spec→plan→TDD→verification-gate shape, and is direct evidence that a BDD-flavored spec layer feeding a TDD implementation loop, closed by a mutation-tested gate, is empirically validated — not just theoretical.
Sources: [thoughtworks.com spec-driven-development-unpacking](https://www.thoughtworks.com/en-us/insights/blog/agile-engineering-practices/spec-driven-development-unpacking-2025-new-engineering-practices), [tessl.io on Sean Grove](https://tessl.io/blog/the-most-valuable-developer-skill-in-2025-writing-code-specifications/), [arxiv.org/abs/2603.17973](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17973v2)

### 6. Critical/skeptical takes — direct counter-arguments
- **Martin Fowler's site, "TDD inside the agent loop - theater or actual value?"**: found TDD-in-agent-loop delivers **minimal or no measurable value**, sometimes worse than non-TDD approaches, because "this is very much about managing a human's fear and giving a human permission to relax. **That doesn't transfer when the agent is doing TDD inside of the loop.**" Agents wrote tautological tests validating implementation against itself; enforcing test-first also suppressed upfront design agents otherwise produced well. This is a direct, credible counter-argument to layering ceremony (BDD or strict TDD) onto agent loops purely for the human-psychological benefits TDD was designed around — the benefit doesn't transfer to a non-human implementer. Your ecosystem's lambda pipeline already forces red-green-commit; this source is a reason to make sure that discipline is earning its keep empirically, not just structurally.
- **"Is SDD Just BDD With an AI Agent?" (isolated-scenario critique, found via search excerpt)**: the core criticism is that BDD's value comes from collaborative *pre-code* discovery among business/dev/test people; when scenarios are written after the fact or unilaterally by/for an AI agent, "they can't serve as specifications, they're just test documentation" — value is lost when the three-amigos collaboration is absent, which is the default case for a solo agent pipeline.
- **Momentic (pro-AI-BDD) counter**: argues AI actually *revives* BDD's original promise by removing the glue-code barrier, letting non-engineers write/modify scenarios directly — but concedes this only holds if there's still a human product/business participant in the loop, not when scenarios are agent-drafted in isolation.
- **ThoughtWorks Radar Vol. 33** (general SDD skepticism): elaborate, opinionated workflows produce spec files "hard to review"; deeper worry that heavy upfront spec formalization is "relearning a bitter lesson — that handcrafting detailed rules for AI ultimately doesn't scale."
- **150–200 standing-instruction degradation finding** (from a dev.to 2026 survey, unverified single-source): frontier models reliably follow ~150-200 standing instructions before compliance degrades — cited as a reason auto-generated, everything-included spec/agent files become "a failure mode wearing a diligence costume." Relevant if adding Given-When-Then to specs meaningfully grows document length/instruction count.
- **Addy Osmani's practical guidance** (widely cited spec-writing post for AI agents): does **not** recommend Given-When-Then/BDD at all. His structure is commands/testing/project-structure/code-style/git-workflow/boundaries, with the guidance "**one real code snippet showing your style beats three paragraphs describing it**" and "incorporate a test plan or even actual tests in your spec" — a lighter-weight, non-scenario-based alternative from a credible practitioner voice, implicitly arguing scenario ceremony is optional overhead for agent-consumed specs.
Sources: [martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/tdd-in-the-agent-loop.html](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/tdd-in-the-agent-loop.html), [momentic.ai/blog/behavior-driven-development](https://momentic.ai/blog/behavior-driven-development), [addyosmani.com/blog/good-spec](https://addyosmani.com/blog/good-spec/)

### Bottom line for your decision
There is real precedent on both sides:
- **For adopting Given-When-Then**: GitHub Spec Kit (the most directly comparable, widely-used tool) bakes it into every spec template; ThoughtWorks explicitly endorses BDD phrasing as the right vocabulary for the spec layer while TDD stays at the unit level (a layered model that maps cleanly onto your spec→plan→TDD→gate pipeline); TDAD's empirical results support scenario-derived test suites reducing regressions.
- **Against, or for caution**: Kiro and Tessl — the two other flagship spec-driven tools — deliberately did *not* adopt Given-When-Then (EARS and plain spec+test pairing respectively), suggesting it's not a consensus default even among spec-driven leaders. The Martin Fowler piece is the sharpest specific warning: ceremony designed for human psychological safety (which is what both TDD's red-green ritual and BDD's collaborative-discovery ritual are for) may not transfer value when an agent — not a human — is the one writing and reading the scenarios. And Osmani, a practitioner writing specifically for agent-consumed specs, omits BDD phrasing entirely in favor of terser structured intent + code examples.

The strongest synthesized position (ThoughtWorks) is that GWT-style scenarios are good **spec-layer vocabulary** for capturing acceptance criteria in a form that both humans and agents can read unambiguously and that maps directly to test cases — independent of whether "collaborative discovery" (BDD's original human-team purpose) is present. If your ecosystem adopts it, the citable justification is "GWT as a precise, testable acceptance-criteria syntax that composes with a TDD implementation loop," not "BDD for cross-functional collaboration" — the latter's value proposition doesn't survive contact with a solo-agent pipeline per the isolated-scenario critique.</result>

## Research Findings: SDD + BDD + TDD Convergence for AI Coding Agents (2025–2026)

### 1. Amazon Kiro — spec-driven, EARS not Gherkin
Kiro (launched July 2025, AWS) runs a three-phase pipeline: requirements → design → tasks, with explicit traceability between phases. Its "Specs" feature converts requirements into **EARS notation** (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) — `WHEN [event] THEN [system] SHALL [response]`, plus `IF`/`WHILE`/`WHERE` variants — not Given-When-Then/Gherkin. EARS criteria are deliberately "unambiguous and testable... easy to translate into test cases." Kiro's hook system separately triggers test-file updates on save/change, but this is automation glue, not a BDD layer. **Direct precedent for structured, machine-parseable acceptance-criteria syntax, but Kiro's own choice was EARS over Given-When-Then** — worth noting since your plugin already resembles the EARS style per your own CLAUDE.md ("EARS-format authoritative rules").
Sources: [kiro.dev/blog/introducing-kiro](https://kiro.dev/blog/introducing-kiro/), [kiro.dev/docs/specs/feature-specs/requirements-first](https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/feature-specs/requirements-first/), [Forbes on Kiro launch](https://www.forbes.com/sites/janakirammsv/2025/07/15/aws-launches-kiro-a-specification-driven-agentic-ide/)

### 2. GitHub Spec Kit — explicit BDD adoption
GitHub's open-source Spec Kit (Sept 2025) pipeline is spec → plan → tasks → implementation, working with 30+ coding agents. Its spec template **explicitly uses Given/When/Then**: "Acceptance Scenarios" per user story are written in that format, each story independently testable and prioritized (P1/P2/P3), plus tagged functional requirements (FR-NNN) and measurable success criteria (SC-NNN). A community extension (spec-kit-reqnroll-bdd) goes further, converting acceptance criteria directly into Gherkin `.feature` files with `@AC-001`-style tags for full BDD tooling integration. **This is the strongest direct precedent for your question** — a major, widely-adopted spec-driven AI tool chose Given-When-Then as its acceptance-scenario format, not EARS-style SHALL statements.
Sources: [github.com/github/spec-kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit), [spec-kit/templates/spec-template.md](https://github.com/github/spec-kit/blob/main/templates/spec-template.md), [github.blog spec-driven-development](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/generative-ai/spec-driven-development-with-ai-get-started-with-a-new-open-source-toolkit/)

### 3. Tessl (Guy Podjarny) — specs "bolstered by tests," not BDD-branded
Tessl's framing: agents "hallucinate APIs, claim success when they've failed, and jump straight into coding without clarifying intent." Their fix is specs as the durable artifact, "bolstered by tests and hard guardrails," with the Tessl Framework pairing specs with auto-generated aligned tests to enforce guardrails as the app evolves, plus a Spec Registry (10,000+ specs) preventing library-API hallucination. Podjarny predicts most 2026 development will be "at least spec-assisted." **Tessl does not use Given-When-Then language publicly** — their vocabulary is spec+test pairing, not scenario-based BDD. Testing is positioned as an enforcement mechanism for specs, not a discovery/collaboration practice.
Sources: [tessl.io/blog/tessl-launches-spec-driven-framework-and-registry](https://tessl.io/blog/tessl-launches-spec-driven-framework-and-registry), [zuplo.com/blog/spec-driven-ai-development](https://zuplo.com/blog/spec-driven-ai-development), [tessl.io/blog/how-tessls-products-pioneer-spec-driven-development](https://tessl.io/blog/how-tessls-products-pioneer-spec-driven-development)

### 4. Other agent products
- **Cursor**: "Plan Mode" enforces Research → Clarify → Plan → Build, explicitly separating planning from coding ("AI coding usually fails when models plan and code at the same time"). No published BDD/Gherkin convention — plans are freeform, refined through iterative questioning until "no room for misinterpretation."
- **Cognition/Devin**: Plan → code → test → ship loop with repo-specific "Playbooks" for conventions; no published spec syntax or BDD adoption found.
- No public methodology found for Windsurf/Cascade, Replit Agent, or Amp specifically addressing BDD/TDD/SDD combination beyond generic "plan then execute" patterns.
Sources: [cursor.com/blog/agent-best-practices](https://cursor.com/blog/agent-best-practices), [cognition.com/blog/introducing-devin](https://cognition.com/blog/introducing-devin)

### 5. Explicit synthesis arguments (BDD+SDD+TDD composing)
- **ThoughtWorks** (Nov 2025, placed SDD in Radar "Assess" ring): explicitly states "**TDD is SDD at the unit level**, and SDD extends this thinking to higher levels." "**BDD is the most direct ancestor of modern SDD**, with Gherkin scenarios as executable specifications." Recommends borrowing BDD's Given/When/Then and "domain-oriented ubiquitous language" for spec-writing, while TDD still drives interface design at the unit level — i.e., **three practices at three altitudes, not competing**. Caveats: no systematic way to eval specs yet; spec drift/hallucination hard to avoid; over-formalized specs risk "waterfall's pitfalls."
- **Sean Grove's "The New Code" (OpenAI, AI Engineer World's Fair 2025)** — the founding talk cited as SDD's origin story: code is only 10-20% of a programmer's value, specs are the real source-of-truth artifact ("shredding the source and carefully version-controlling the binary" describes prompt-then-discard workflows). Doesn't address BDD/TDD directly but is the philosophical root everyone else cites.
- **TDAD (Test-Driven Agentic Development, arXiv 2603.17973)**: an explicit synthesis paper — behavioral specs compiled into executable test suites by one agent, a second agent iterates implementation against them, mutation testing validates the tests. Reduced regressions 70% (6.08%→1.82%) vs vanilla baseline. This is very close to your ecosystem's spec→plan→TDD→verification-gate shape, and is direct evidence that a BDD-flavored spec layer feeding a TDD implementation loop, closed by a mutation-tested gate, is empirically validated — not just theoretical.
Sources: [thoughtworks.com spec-driven-development-unpacking](https://www.thoughtworks.com/en-us/insights/blog/agile-engineering-practices/spec-driven-development-unpacking-2025-new-engineering-practices), [tessl.io on Sean Grove](https://tessl.io/blog/the-most-valuable-developer-skill-in-2025-writing-code-specifications/), [arxiv.org/abs/2603.17973](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17973v2)

### 6. Critical/skeptical takes — direct counter-arguments
- **Martin Fowler's site, "TDD inside the agent loop - theater or actual value?"**: found TDD-in-agent-loop delivers **minimal or no measurable value**, sometimes worse than non-TDD approaches, because "this is very much about managing a human's fear and giving a human permission to relax. **That doesn't transfer when the agent is doing TDD inside of the loop.**" Agents wrote tautological tests validating implementation against itself; enforcing test-first also suppressed upfront design agents otherwise produced well. This is a direct, credible counter-argument to layering ceremony (BDD or strict TDD) onto agent loops purely for the human-psychological benefits TDD was designed around — the benefit doesn't transfer to a non-human implementer. Your ecosystem's lambda pipeline already forces red-green-commit; this source is a reason to make sure that discipline is earning its keep empirically, not just structurally.
- **"Is SDD Just BDD With an AI Agent?" (isolated-scenario critique, found via search excerpt)**: the core criticism is that BDD's value comes from collaborative *pre-code* discovery among business/dev/test people; when scenarios are written after the fact or unilaterally by/for an AI agent, "they can't serve as specifications, they're just test documentation" — value is lost when the three-amigos collaboration is absent, which is the default case for a solo agent pipeline.
- **Momentic (pro-AI-BDD) counter**: argues AI actually *revives* BDD's original promise by removing the glue-code barrier, letting non-engineers write/modify scenarios directly — but concedes this only holds if there's still a human product/business participant in the loop, not when scenarios are agent-drafted in isolation.
- **ThoughtWorks Radar Vol. 33** (general SDD skepticism): elaborate, opinionated workflows produce spec files "hard to review"; deeper worry that heavy upfront spec formalization is "relearning a bitter lesson — that handcrafting detailed rules for AI ultimately doesn't scale."
- **150–200 standing-instruction degradation finding** (from a dev.to 2026 survey, unverified single-source): frontier models reliably follow ~150-200 standing instructions before compliance degrades — cited as a reason auto-generated, everything-included spec/agent files become "a failure mode wearing a diligence costume." Relevant if adding Given-When-Then to specs meaningfully grows document length/instruction count.
- **Addy Osmani's practical guidance** (widely cited spec-writing post for AI agents): does **not** recommend Given-When-Then/BDD at all. His structure is commands/testing/project-structure/code-style/git-workflow/boundaries, with the guidance "**one real code snippet showing your style beats three paragraphs describing it**" and "incorporate a test plan or even actual tests in your spec" — a lighter-weight, non-scenario-based alternative from a credible practitioner voice, implicitly arguing scenario ceremony is optional overhead for agent-consumed specs.
Sources: [martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/tdd-in-the-agent-loop.html](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/tdd-in-the-agent-loop.html), [momentic.ai/blog/behavior-driven-development](https://momentic.ai/blog/behavior-driven-development), [addyosmani.com/blog/good-spec](https://addyosmani.com/blog/good-spec/)

### Bottom line for your decision
There is real precedent on both sides:
- **For adopting Given-When-Then**: GitHub Spec Kit (the most directly comparable, widely-used tool) bakes it into every spec template; ThoughtWorks explicitly endorses BDD phrasing as the right vocabulary for the spec layer while TDD stays at the unit level (a layered model that maps cleanly onto your spec→plan→TDD→gate pipeline); TDAD's empirical results support scenario-derived test suites reducing regressions.
- **Against, or for caution**: Kiro and Tessl — the two other flagship spec-driven tools — deliberately did *not* adopt Given-When-Then (EARS and plain spec+test pairing respectively), suggesting it's not a consensus default even among spec-driven leaders. The Martin Fowler piece is the sharpest specific warning: ceremony designed for human psychological safety (which is what both TDD's red-green ritual and BDD's collaborative-discovery ritual are for) may not transfer value when an agent — not a human — is the one writing and reading the scenarios. And Osmani, a practitioner writing specifically for agent-consumed specs, omits BDD phrasing entirely in favor of terser structured intent + code examples.

The strongest synthesized position (ThoughtWorks) is that GWT-style scenarios are good **spec-layer vocabulary** for capturing acceptance criteria in a form that both humans and agents can read unambiguously and that maps directly to test cases — independent of whether "collaborative discovery" (BDD's original human-team purpose) is present. If your ecosystem adopts it, the citable justification is "GWT as a precise, testable acceptance-criteria syntax that composes with a TDD implementation loop," not "BDD for cross-functional collaboration" — the latter's value proposition doesn't survive contact with a solo-agent pipeline per the isolated-scenario critique.</result>
